submission.title: EditSleuth: A Dataset of Grounded Reasoning Chains for Image-Edit Forensics
submission.venue: NeurIPS 2026 Datasets & Benchmarks (Evaluations and Datasets) Track

findings.title: The pilot's headline claim is arithmetically false: chain-target beats label-only on one of three fields, not two, and the abstract/intro/conclusion escalate this to an unqualified "matches"
findings.location: §5.4 "Results" (p8); Table 3 (p8); §5.4 "Interpretation" (p9); Abstract (p1); §1 (p2); Contribution (iv) (p2)
findings.evidence: §5.4: "Conditional on successful extraction, chain-target obtains 33.4%/37.2%/40.8% on category/spatial/bin, compared with label-only's 39.7%/42.2%/33.1%. Thus, chain-target matches or exceeds label-only on two of three fields once parseability is controlled for." Table 3 raw values: chain-target 22.5/67.4, 29.7/79.9, 28.0/68.6; label-only 37.1/93.6, 42.2/100, 33.1/100. My recomputation of accuracy/extraction: chain 22.5/67.4 = 33.38%, 29.7/79.9 = 37.17%, 28.0/68.6 = 40.82%; label 37.1/93.6 = 39.64%, 42.2/100 = 42.20%, 33.1/100 = 33.10%. Abstract: "chain-as-target supervision matches a label-only baseline on classification accuracy among parseable answers." §5.4 Interpretation: "When outputs are parseable, chain-target supervision matches label-only training on category, spatial, and difficulty classification, indicating no loss in underlying prediction quality." §5.4 "Effect of additional training": "chain-target regresses: spatial extraction recall drops 79.9→67.0%, and conditional spatial/bin accuracy falls from 37.2→32.5% and 40.8→34.4%" while "Label-only improves modestly (category 37.1→39.6%, bin 33.1→34.7%)."
findings.claim: The paper's own conditional numbers show chain-target LOSING to label-only on category (33.4 vs 39.7, a 6.3-point / 16% relative deficit) and on spatial (37.2 vs 42.2, 5.0 points), and winning only on difficulty bin (40.8 vs 33.1). That is one of three, not "two of three." The Interpretation paragraph then strengthens the already-wrong claim to "matches ... on category, spatial, and difficulty classification, indicating no loss in underlying prediction quality" — i.e. all three — and the abstract, introduction and Contribution (iv) inherit the unqualified version. The two-epoch re-run reverses even the single win: chain-target's conditional bin accuracy falls to 34.4% against label-only's 34.7%, so at two epochs chain-target trails on every field.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the paper's only learning result and the sole support for Contribution (iv) ("validates chain-as-target supervision at the classification level"). Once the arithmetic is done correctly, the pilot supports the opposite reading — chain supervision is worse on the two fields with the most semantic content and better only on the one field that is not comparable across the train/eval datasets (see finding bin-not-comparable). No amount of rewording rescues "matches"; the numbers are printed in the same sentence that misreads them.
findings.verifier_note: I recomputed every cell from Table 3 (p8) and the paper's own conditional numbers reproduce exactly from integer counts: chain 119/356=33.4%, 157/422=37.2%, 148/362=40.8%; label-only 196/494=39.7%, 223/528=42.2%, 175/528=33.1%. On face value chain-target trails by 6.3 points (category) and 5.0 points (spatial) and leads by 7.7 points (bin) — one of three, not 'two of three.' I tried three rebuttals and none survives. (a) 'Rounding/typo': the gap is 5-6 points, not rounding. (b) 'Matches means statistically indistinguishable': running the tests the paper never ran, category z=-1.86 (p=0.063) and spatial z=-1.57 (p=0.118) are both n.s. while bin z=+2.36 (p=0.018) is significant — that reading gives three of three, not two, and is nowhere stated. (c) 'Category is a loss, spatial a match, bin a win = two of three': this is the only reading that yields 2, but it requires an unstated tolerance that calls 5.0 points a match and 6.3 points a loss. Decisively, the paper contradicts itself internally: §5.4 Results says 'two of three fields' (conceding one loss) while §5.4 Interpretation says chain-target 'matches label-only training on category, spatial, and difficulty classification, indicating no loss in underlying prediction quality' (all three), and the Abstract, §1 and Contribution (iv) carry the unqualified version. One caveat on the reviewer's tail: at two epochs the paper reports no chain-target category number (only 'conditional spatial/bin accuracy falls from 37.2→32.5% and 40.8→34.4%'), so 'trails on every field' is inference, and 34.4 vs 34.7 is ~1.6 examples, a tie rather than a reversal.

findings.title: The abstract's compensating benefit — "grounded explanatory prose" — is contradicted by the paper's own §6 limitation and by Table 3's extraction recalls
findings.location: Abstract (p1); §5.4 "Interpretation" (p9); §6 bullet "Unverified inference-time chain faithfulness" (p9); Table 3 (p8)
findings.evidence: Abstract: "while additionally yielding grounded explanatory prose that label-only supervision cannot produce." §5.4: "Its added benefit is grounded prose: all chain-target generations include evidence such as mask area, structural-change score, and category-level forensic priors, which label-only training cannot produce." §6: "The pilot model learns to emit six-step chains, including numerical fields, but does not compute those fields from the underlying artifacts. Thus, generated triplet-grounded statements are model estimates rather than verified quantities; measuring this drift remains open." Table 3, chain-target "extracted": category 67.4%, spatial descriptor 79.9%, difficulty bin 68.6%.
findings.claim: The Abstract's 'grounded explanatory prose' describes the pilot model's output, but §6 states the model 'does not compute those fields from the underlying artifacts' and that its triplet-grounded statements 'are model estimates rather than verified quantities' whose drift is unmeasured — so the word 'grounded' is earned by the dataset's construction but not by the model outputs the Abstract attributes it to. Separately, §5.4's 'all chain-target generations include evidence such as mask area, structural-change score, and category-level forensic priors' is asserted without measurement: Table 3 reports extraction recall only for category (67.4%), spatial descriptor (79.9%) and difficulty bin (68.6%), none of which is one of the three evidence items claimed, and 20-33% of generations already fail those parsers.
findings.why_it_matters: Since the classification claim collapses (see two-of-three-miscount), "grounded prose" is the only remaining justification in the abstract for preferring chain supervision. It rests on an untested property that §6 explicitly flags as unmeasured, and on a universal quantifier ("all") that Table 3 falsifies. As stated, the abstract asserts a benefit the paper has no measurement of.
findings.verifier_note: Part (1) survives: the Abstract's 'additionally yielding grounded explanatory prose' is a property of the fine-tuned model's output, and §6 explicitly denies it — 'The pilot model ... does not compute those fields from the underlying artifacts. Thus, generated triplet-grounded statements are model estimates rather than verified quantities; measuring this drift remains open.' Part (2) does not survive contact with the table. §5.4's sentence claims the generations include 'mask area, structural-change score, and category-level forensic priors' — those are Steps 2, 3 and 5, and Table 3 reports extraction recall for category (Step 4, 67.4%), spatial descriptor (Step 2, 79.9%) and difficulty bin (Step 6, 68.6%). None of the three claimed evidence items has a reported recall. §5.4 Metrics defines extraction as 'the fraction of generations from which each field can be parsed' — a generation can emit 'the mask covers roughly 30% of the image' and a Step-5 prior while still failing the category parser (e.g. an out-of-vocabulary category string). So 'false on the paper's own table' overreaches; the correct charge is that the universal claim is unmeasured and sits alongside 20-33% field-parse failures. I also note the paper's §2 analogy is imperfect: unlike the frontier-LLM chains it criticizes, the pilot VLM does observe the images; what it does not do is compute the numbers.

findings.title: "We find no faithfulness violations" is circular by construction, its sample does not cover the cases it reports, and Appendix D's own showcase chains contain prior/content contradictions — including on Pico-Banana, where the paper says priors are "always appropriate"
findings.location: §5.3 (p8); §3.4 (p5); Appendix D (pp14–17), specifically the human_centric, style_transfer, scene_transformation, geometric and text_edit exemplars
findings.evidence: §5.3: "We inspect a stratified sample of ∼50 Pico-Banana triplets across difficulty bins... We find no faithfulness violations: all numerical claims, including mask area fraction, structural-change score, and difficulty bin, match upstream artifacts by construction. Forensic priors are visually plausible except in two MagicBrush cases where keyword rules misclassified the edit semantics. On Pico-Banana, where categories come from curated labels, priors are always appropriate." §3.4: "template-driven composition only states claims licensed by upstream artifacts." Appendix D, human_centric ([source=dataset_label], i.e. Pico-Banana): Step 2 "The mask of changed pixels covers roughly 100% of the image and spans the entire image" vs Step 5 "changes confined to a person, with the surrounding scene preserved." Appendix D, style_transfer ([source=dataset_label]): instruction is "applying a vibrant, high-contrast color grade with crisp details, brightening the overall scene" vs Step 5 "global texture and brushstroke patterns inconsistent with natural photography" — while §3.3 justifies splitting photometric from style_transfer precisely because "global tone, grain, and color shifts have different forensic signatures." Appendix D, scene_transformation: Step 2 "roughly 13% of the image and is centered" vs Step 5 "affect the whole scene coherently rather than any single object." Appendix D, geometric (confidence 0.85): instruction "make the piece of paper hanging on the wall a mirror," Step 2 "roughly 14% ... concentrated in the upper-left region" vs Step 5 "canvas-level transformations such as cropped boundaries, scaled content, or extrapolated regions outside the original frame, rather than localized object edits." Appendix D, text_edit: Step 2 "is centered in the image" vs Step 3 "the edit region is diffuse or split across multiple sub-regions."
findings.claim: §5.3's audit is weak in two verifiable ways. First, its numerical half is non-falsifiable as framed — the paper says the numbers 'match upstream artifacts by construction,' so inspecting 50 chains restates Stage E's determinism rather than testing it. Second, the claim 'On Pico-Banana, where categories come from curated labels, priors are always appropriate' fails on the paper's own showcase: the Appendix D human_centric chain (source=dataset_label, i.e. Pico-Banana) reports scope=global and 'roughly 100% of the image ... spans the entire image' in Step 2, yet Step 5 asserts the category prior 'changes confined to a person, with the surrounding scene preserved.' Under §5.3's own stated criterion ('whether category-level forensic priors match the visible edit') this prior does not match; under the alternative reading that a prior is 'appropriate' whenever it is the template for the assigned category, the audit is vacuous. Additionally, the two reported violations are 'MagicBrush cases' while the stated sample is '∼50 Pico-Banana triplets,' so those cases have no stated denominator or protocol.
findings.why_it_matters: Auditable faithfulness is the paper's central differentiator (Abstract: rationales "whose faithfulness is difficult to verify"; §2: "the first dataset to combine edited-image triplets with auditable reasoning-chain supervision"). §5.3 is the only faithfulness evidence in the paper, and it is both non-falsifiable as designed and empirically contradicted by the appendix the reader is pointed to. If the paper's best-case, hand-selected exemplars teach a model that a 100%-of-image mask is "confined to a person, with the surrounding scene preserved," the supervision signal is not faithful in any sense a forensic user would accept.
findings.verifier_note: Two of four sub-claims hold, two do not. Holds: (i) the numerical half of the audit is near-tautological — the paper itself writes the numerical claims 'match upstream artifacts by construction' (§5.3) and §3.4 says 'template-driven composition only states claims licensed by upstream artifacts'; the residual discriminating power is limited to template-instantiation bugs, which the paper does not claim to be testing. (ii) the sample is stated as '∼50 Pico-Banana triplets' yet the only violations reported are 'two MagicBrush cases,' which have no stated denominator or sampling protocol — genuine under-specification. Does not hold: (iii) 'far more than two MagicBrush cases' conflates samples — inside Appendix D exactly two MagicBrush (source=rule_based) exemplars carry mismatched priors (scene_transformation: 13% centered mask vs a prior about changes that 'affect the whole scene coherently'; geometric: 'make the piece of paper hanging on the wall a mirror' vs a prior about 'canvas-level transformations'), which is consistent with, not far more than, the paper's count, and Appendix D is a different sample from the ∼50. (iv) the alleged 'mutually contradictory localization' is a misreading: §3.4 defines Step 2 as 'spatial localization using a coarse descriptor' (where the mask sits) and Step 3 as 'magnitude from structural-change and compactness scores' (how dispersed it is); a mask can be centered or upper-left and still be split across sub-regions, so 'centered' vs 'diffuse or split' is not a contradiction. On the Pico-Banana claim, only human_centric is airtight (style_transfer is arguable).

findings.title: The one field where chain-target wins (difficulty bin) is measured across two datasets whose bin labels the paper itself defines to be non-transferable, and the baseline on it sits at chance
findings.location: §3.2 "Tertile binning" (p4); §4.3 (p6); Table 3 (p8); Appendix D difficulty scores (pp14–17)
findings.evidence: §3.2: "We compute the empirical 33rd and 66th percentiles of D on each dataset and bin triplets accordingly. Binning is dataset-internal so that easy/medium/hard labels remain meaningful relative to corpus statistics rather than absolute thresholds." §4.3: Pico-Banana "tertile cutoffs at 0.406 and 0.504." Appendix D MagicBrush exemplars (source=rule_based/fallback) span difficulty score 0.10–0.28, with the three labelled hard at 0.28, 0.24 and 0.23 — every MagicBrush example, including all hard ones, lies below Pico-Banana's easy cutoff of 0.406. §5.4 Setup: training is "on a stratified Pico-Banana subset"; evaluation "uses MagicBrush dev (n= 528)." Table 3: label-only difficulty bin accuracy = 33.1%.
findings.claim: §3.2 makes difficulty bins dataset-internal percentiles ('relative to corpus statistics rather than absolute thresholds'), so the bin label the model is trained on (Pico-Banana tertiles, cutoffs 0.406/0.504, §4.3) and the bin label it is scored against (MagicBrush dev tertiles) denote different quantities, and the paper never reports MagicBrush's cutoffs or flags the incomparability. The nine MagicBrush chains in Appendix D span difficulty 0.10-0.28 — including all three labelled hard (0.28, 0.24, 0.23) — entirely below Pico-Banana's easy cutoff, consistent with σ_MB=0.066 vs σ_PB=0.109 (§5.1). Table 3's difficulty-bin column should be read against a 33.3% chance level that the paper never states: label-only's 33.1% is exactly chance, and chain-target's 40.8% conditional is ~7 points above it.
findings.why_it_matters: After the two-of-three arithmetic is corrected, this single field is the entire empirical basis for any claim that chain supervision helps. It is the least interpretable of the three metrics: the ground-truth labels are not commensurable across the train/eval split, and the competitor is a null model. A rebuttal cannot repair this without re-running the evaluation with a shared difficulty anchoring.
findings.verifier_note: The core is verified and I could not defeat it: §3.2 states 'Binning is dataset-internal so that easy/medium/hard labels remain meaningful relative to corpus statistics rather than absolute thresholds'; §5.1 confirms bins are computed 'separately for each scorer, on Pico-Banana (n=257,725) and MagicBrush dev (n=528)'; §5.4 trains on Pico-Banana (cutoffs 0.406/0.504, §4.3) and evaluates on MagicBrush dev. The bin label therefore denotes a within-corpus percentile that no image-conditioned model can recover, and MagicBrush cutoffs are never reported (grep confirms no MagicBrush mean or cutoffs anywhere). Chance on a tertile-balanced 3-way task is 33.3%; label-only scores 33.1%, and neither the chance level nor any majority/random baseline appears anywhere in the paper. The one overreach is 'whose entire support lies below Pico-Banana's easy cutoff': that rests on nine Appendix D exemplars (0.10-0.28, hard ones at 0.28/0.24/0.23) plus σ_MB=0.066, not on any reported MagicBrush distribution, so 'entire support' is not established — the authors could rebut that Appendix D is not a random sample.

findings.title: Nearly half of the MagicBrush evaluation labels are categories the model was never trained to emit, so a constant "other" predictor beats every number in Table 3; no trivial baseline is reported anywhere
findings.location: Table 1 (p6); §5.4 "Setup" and "Results" (p8); Table 3 (p8); §4.2 (p5)
findings.evidence: Table 1, MagicBrush dev: other = 235 (44.5%), background_change = 11 (2.1%); total 528. §5.4 Setup: training is "balanced across 11 non-other categories and three difficulty bins" — other is excluded by construction, and Table 1 shows Pico-Banana has 0 background_change. Table 3 best category accuracy: label-only 37.1% raw, 39.7% conditional. §5.4: "Absolute accuracies are limited by noisy MagicBrush dev labels ... Thus, the relative model comparison is more reliable than the absolute accuracy values." §4.2, on the spatial-descriptor label distribution: "centered covers 89% of local edits" and 30.4% of triplets are global.
findings.claim: 246 of 528 MagicBrush dev examples (46.6%) carry a gold category — other (235) or background_change (11) — that the Pico-Banana training subset contains zero instances of (§5.4 Setup: 'balanced across 11 non-other categories'; Table 1: Pico-Banana background_change = 0), effectively capping category accuracy at 53.4%; and a zero-parameter constant 'other' predictor scores 44.5%, beating every category number in Table 3 (chain 22.5%/33.4%, label-only 37.1%/39.7%). The paper reports no majority-class, random, or zero-shot baseline for any field, and attributes the low absolutes to 'noisy MagicBrush dev labels' without noting that its own training design makes 46.6% of the evaluation unreachable. The same baseline gap exists for the spatial-descriptor column, whose MagicBrush gold marginal is never reported.
findings.why_it_matters: Contribution (iv) claims the pilot "validates chain-as-target supervision at the classification level." Without any baseline, and against an eval set where a one-line constant beats both fine-tuned models on the primary field, the table cannot support a validation claim in either the relative or absolute direction. This also compounds the two-of-three error: both models may be operating below trivial baselines on the field where the comparison was miscounted.
findings.verifier_note: The category half is airtight and I could not dent it. Table 1's MagicBrush dev column sums to 528 and gives other=235 and background_change=11; (235+11)/528 = 46.59%, leaving a 53.4% ceiling, and §5.4 Setup trains on Pico-Banana 'balanced across 11 non-other categories' while Table 1 shows Pico-Banana has zero background_change — so neither class is ever seen. A constant 'other' predictor scores 44.5%, above label-only's 37.1% raw and 39.7% conditional and far above chain-target's 22.5%/33.4%. A grep for 'chance', 'majority', 'zero-shot', 'random baseline' returns nothing in the paper, so the missing-baseline charge holds. Two tails are weaker. (a) 'Solely' overstates slightly: §5.4 does name the driver — '"ground truth" comes from the same rule classifier with a 44% fallback rate' — it just frames it as label noise rather than as an unreachable-class ceiling and never computes the trivial baseline. (b) The spatial half is speculative: §4.2's ~92% concentration (30.4% global + 89% of the 69.6% local = 92.3%) is the Pico-Banana training distribution, whereas Table 3's spatial column is scored on MagicBrush dev, whose descriptor marginal is never reported — so a constant predictor's score there is unknown, not demonstrably competitive.

findings.title: "Pico-Banana covers all 11 non-other categories" is contradicted by Table 1 and by Table 1's own caption, and makes the stated §5.4 training design impossible
findings.location: §4.1 (p5); Table 1 and its caption (p6); §5.4 "Setup" (p8)
findings.evidence: §4.1: "Pico-Banana covers all 11 non-other categories, with no category above 21% and the smallest non-zero category, text_edit, at 4.1%." Table 1, background_change row: Pico-Banana count 0, 0.0%, difficulty cells "—". Table 1 caption: "background_change is reserved for foreground-preserving background swaps, which appear in MagicBrush but not Pico-Banana; categories with zero Pico-Banana coverage have undefined difficulty distributions and are marked '—'." §5.4 Setup: training is "on a stratified Pico-Banana subset (ntrain ∼20,000), balanced across 11 non-other categories and three difficulty bins."
findings.claim: Pico-Banana covers 10 of 11 non-other categories, not all 11 — the paper's own table and caption say so explicitly, and the §4.1 hedge "smallest non-zero category" tacitly concedes a zero category exists. The error is not merely cosmetic: §5.4 claims the pilot training set is "balanced across 11 non-other categories" drawn from Pico-Banana, which is arithmetically impossible when one of those 11 has zero Pico-Banana instances. Either the training set is balanced over 10 categories (so the setup description is wrong) or it drew from a source not described.
findings.why_it_matters: Coverage of the 12-category taxonomy is a stated contribution (ii), and the training-set composition is load-bearing for reading Table 3 — it determines which of the 528 eval examples are even answerable. A factual claim about the dataset's own composition contradicting its own table is the kind of error that makes a reviewer distrust the rest of the characterization, and it cannot be argued away.
findings.verifier_note: Verified verbatim and I can find no rebuttal that saves the sentence. §4.1: 'Pico-Banana covers all 11 non-other categories, with no category above 21% and the smallest non-zero category, text_edit, at 4.1%.' Table 1's background_change row gives Pico-Banana count 0, 0.0%, difficulty '—'; the caption says background_change 'appear[s] in MagicBrush but not Pico-Banana'; and §3.3 says the same ('present in MagicBrush but absent from Pico-Banana's taxonomy'). So the paper contradicts itself three ways over, and the hedge 'smallest non-zero category' concedes a zero category exists. The only available rebuttal — 'typo for 10' — does not dissolve the finding because the same wrong count is load-bearing in §5.4 Setup, where the pilot training set is described as 'a stratified Pico-Banana subset (ntrain ∼20,000), balanced across 11 non-other categories,' which cannot be true of a Pico-Banana draw containing zero background_change. This also underwrites the 53.4% category ceiling in the ceiling finding.

findings.title: No field in Table 3 has human ground truth; the evaluation measures whether the model reproduces the pipeline's own deterministic outputs, and for two of three fields the label source is never stated
findings.evidence: §5.4: "the set lacks curated category annotations, so 'ground truth' comes from the same rule classifier with a 44% fallback rate (§4.1). Manual inspection reveals several questionable label assignments." §3.3: MagicBrush categories come from "an ordered regex classifier over explicit edit verbs, conversational frames, domain keywords, and geometric operations." §5.3 confirms this classifier errs: "two MagicBrush cases where keyword rules misclassified the edit semantics." §5.4 Metrics defines extraction and scoring but never states where the spatial-descriptor or difficulty-bin gold labels for MagicBrush dev come from; the only candidates in the paper are Stage B and Stage C outputs.
findings.claim: Table 3's three gold-label columns are either pipeline outputs or of unstated provenance. The paper concedes the category gold is Stage D's regex classifier — the same classifier §5.3 documents as misclassifying MagicBrush edits — so that column measures agreement with a known-imperfect rule set rather than forensic correctness. The difficulty-bin gold can only be Stage C output, and §5.4 Metrics never states where the spatial-descriptor gold comes from, even though Appendix A records that MagicBrush ships a human 'ground-truth manipulation mask' that the paper uses for the §3.1 IoU calibration and Appendix E figures. The evaluation should therefore be read as pipeline-reproduction accuracy, and the label provenance for two of three columns should be stated.
findings.why_it_matters: Contribution (iv) and the abstract present Table 3 as evidence about classification quality. If the targets are the pipeline's own outputs, high accuracy would demonstrate distillation of a regex plus a thresholding routine, not forensic capability — and low accuracy (as observed) is uninterpretable. Under-specification here is not a writing nit: it decides what the paper's only learning experiment measures.
findings.verifier_note: The strongest component is disclosed by the paper itself, which blunts the 'gotcha' framing: §5.4 states outright that 'the set lacks curated category annotations, so "ground truth" comes from the same rule classifier with a 44% fallback rate (§4.1). Manual inspection reveals several questionable label assignments,' and immediately cautions that 'the relative model comparison is more reliable than the absolute accuracy values.' The novel component holds but is under-specification rather than error: §5.4 Metrics defines extraction and scoring but never states where the MagicBrush spatial-descriptor or difficulty-bin gold labels come from. The reviewer's 'by elimination they must be Stage B/Stage C outputs' is too strong for the spatial column, because the reviewer's own evidence shows an alternative existed — Appendix A records that MagicBrush ships 'mask_img (a ground-truth manipulation mask),' which the paper does use elsewhere (the §3.1 IoU calibration and the Appendix E mask comparisons). For difficulty bin the elimination does hold: Stage C is the only difficulty source in the paper.

findings.title: The "rank-2 collapse" claim, repeated in the abstract, intro, §3.2, §5.1 and the conclusion, is never supported by any rank, eigenvalue or PCA evidence, and V1's weights are never stated so the ablation is not reproducible
findings.location: Abstract (p1); §1 (p2); Contribution (iii) (p2); §3.2 (p4); §5.1 (p7); §7 (p9)
findings.evidence: Abstract: "a naive four-component difficulty formulation suffers from a rank-2 correlation collapse among magnitude features." §3.2: "the magnitude trio collapses to rank-2 on both datasets (pairwise |r| ∈[0.68,0.91]), suppressing the variance of the combined score under weighted summation." §5.1: "magnitude-term correlations are [0.78,0.91] on MagicBrush versus [0.68,0.85] on Pico-Banana" and "This compresses the combined score to roughly 1/4–1/5 of a single component's variance." §7: "replacing a rank-collapsed magnitude trio with one canonical magnitude term plus compactness." Reported σ values: V1 Pico-Banana σ = 0.070; s_struct σ = 0.244 (§4.3).
findings.claim: The only evidence offered for a rank claim is a range of pairwise absolute correlations, which does not determine the rank or effective rank of a correlation matrix; no eigenvalues, singular values or explained-variance figures appear anywhere in the paper. Separately, the quantitative gloss "roughly 1/4–1/5 of a single component's variance" does not reproduce from the paper's own numbers under either reading: 0.070/0.244 = 0.287 (≈1/3.5) in standard deviation, and (0.070/0.244)² = 0.082 (≈1/12) in variance. Finally, V1's four weights are never given anywhere in the paper, so the σV1 = 0.070 vs σV2 = 0.109 comparison cannot be reproduced or checked for apples-to-apples weighting.
findings.why_it_matters: The rank-2 finding is elevated to the abstract, to Contribution (iii) ("Empirical validation of the pipeline's design choices: the rank-2 collapse motivating V2 difficulty") and to the conclusion. Presenting an unmeasured linear-algebraic property as an empirical finding, with a supporting ratio that contradicts the paper's own statistics and an unspecified baseline formula, means the headline design justification is not verifiable by a reader.
findings.verifier_note: All three sub-claims verified and I could not refute any. (a) A grep for 'eigen', 'singular', 'principal', 'PCA', 'explained var' returns zero hits in the entire paper; the sole evidence for the rank claim is 'pairwise |r| ∈[0.68,0.91]' (§3.2) and the per-dataset ranges in §5.1. Worse for the authors, I computed the spectrum of correlation matrices matching the sign structure §5.1 describes (s_struct-s_perc positive, both negatively correlated with s_loc): for (0.85, -0.68, -0.75) the eigenvalues are 2.52/0.34/0.14, participation rank 1.39, top eigenvalue 84% of the trace; for the MagicBrush-like (0.91, -0.78, -0.85) they are 2.69/0.23/0.08, rank 1.23. The structure implied by the reported correlations is effectively rank-1, not rank-2 — and V2's remedy, retaining 'one canonical magnitude term' (§7), presupposes rank-1, since discarding two of three components from a genuinely rank-2 subspace would lose a dimension. (b) The 1/4-1/5 gloss does not reproduce: 0.070/0.244 = 0.287 (~1/3.5) in standard deviation, (0.070/0.244)^2 = 0.082 (~1/12) in variance. (c) A grep for weights returns only V2's '(wS, wC, wI) = (0.55,0.25,0.20)'; V1's four weights appear nowhere, so σV1 = 0.070 cannot be reproduced or checked for comparable weighting.

findings.title: Contribution (iii) validates the difficulty score only by score dispersion; nothing in the paper shows the score predicts detection difficulty, and no result is ever broken down by difficulty bin
findings.location: Abstract (p1); Contribution (iii) (p2); §4.3 (p6); §5.1 (p7); Table 3 (p8)
findings.evidence: Abstract: "a simplified three-component formulation substantially increases score dispersion on both Pico-Banana and MagicBrush." Contribution (iii): "Empirical validation of the pipeline's design choices: the rank-2 collapse motivating V2 difficulty ... and the within-category discrimination of the difficulty score." §4.3: "We qualitatively validated the bins by inspecting a stratified sample of ∼50 Pico-Banana triplets. Clear, well-localized edits typically fell in easy or medium, while saturated whole-image masks or visually diffuse edits fell in hard." §4.3 also promises: "the reported marginals provide a natural evaluation breakdown: strong performance on easy text_edit but weak performance on hard geometric implies a different failure mode." Table 3 reports only aggregate accuracy — no per-difficulty rows.
findings.claim: The paper's only quantitative support for the difficulty score is dispersion (+55%/+94% σ) and a qualitative inspection, neither of which is a validity criterion for detection difficulty. Tertile bins are assigned by empirical percentiles (§3.2), so σ does not affect which triplets are labelled easy/medium/hard; the §4.3 inspection ('saturated whole-image masks or visually diffuse edits fell in hard') restates the formula, since D is built from 1-SSIM and 1-compactness; and the one experiment that could have tested the score externally, the §5.4 pilot, reports no per-difficulty breakdown even though §4.3 proposes precisely that as the score's downstream use. No detector-error or human-difficulty criterion is measured anywhere.
findings.why_it_matters: The word "difficulty" carries a semantic commitment: that examples binned hard are harder for a detector. Nothing in the paper tests that, so a user stratifying a curriculum by these bins would be stratifying by edit magnitude and mask compactness under a misleading name. Contribution (iii) claims empirical validation for a property that is never measured against any downstream criterion.
findings.verifier_note: The underlying issue is real but the stated argument has a defeasible step. 'Standard deviation ... can be increased by any monotone rescaling' invites an easy rebuttal: V1 and V2 are both convex combinations of components in [0,1] with weights summing to one (§3.2), so they share a bounded scale and V2 is not an arbitrary rescaling of V1 — the σ comparison is not meaningless. And the paper offers a scale-invariant version in the Figure 2 caption ('tertile bins separated by ∼1σ'), which I verified: (0.504-0.406)/0.109 = 0.90σ. The stronger, non-refutable points are the ones the reviewer states second: (i) tertile bins are rank-based (§3.2, 'empirical 33rd and 66th percentiles'), so dispersion is orthogonal to which triplets land in which bin; (ii) the §4.3 check is circular, since D = 0.55·(1-SSIM) + 0.25·(1-compactness) + 0.20·s_instr, so 'saturated whole-image masks or visually diffuse edits fell in hard' restates the formula's inputs; and (iii) Table 3 has no per-difficulty rows despite §4.3 proposing exactly that breakdown ('strong performance on easy text_edit but weak performance on hard geometric implies a different failure mode'). Also worth noting the ∼0.9σ tertile separation is close to the 0.86σ any near-normal score would give, so it is weak evidence too.

findings.title: §3.2 sells compactness as "a genuinely independent spatial signal" while §5.1 measures r = −0.44 between exactly those two components — the same anti-correlation mechanism the paper blames for V1's collapse
findings.location: §3.2 (p4); §5.1 "Why the trio collapses" and following paragraph (p7); §6 first bullet (p9)
findings.evidence: §3.2: "V2 retains sstruct as the magnitude representative and adds compactness as a genuinely independent spatial signal." §5.1: "The collapse is driven by the strong negative correlation between sloc = 1−mask_area_frac and the two magnitude terms. Large edits raise sstruct and sperc but lower sloc ... causing partial cancellation in the weighted sum." §5.1: "One residual issue remains: on Pico-Banana local edits, V2's image-derived components, sstruct and scompact, show a moderate negative correlation (r=−0.44)." Weights (§3.2): wS = 0.55, wC = 0.25 — together 0.80 of the score.
findings.claim: §3.2's description of compactness as 'a genuinely independent spatial signal' is contradicted by the paper's own §5.1 measurement of r = -0.44 between s_struct and s_compact on Pico-Banana local edits — the two terms carrying 0.80 of V2's weight. The paper attributes that correlation to 'Stage B mask-quality artifacts' without noting that, whatever its cause, an anti-correlated pair inside a weighted sum reproduces in weaker form the cancellation mechanism §5.1 identifies as V1's defect, and it states no criterion for why |r| = 0.44 is tolerable when |r| ∈ [0.68,0.91] was disqualifying. The claim should read 'less correlated than the magnitude trio,' not 'genuinely independent.'
findings.why_it_matters: This is the design rationale for the production scorer used on all 257,725 released triplets and one of three headline construction findings in the conclusion. The claimed independence is measured to be absent in the paper's own ablation, three pages later. §6 discloses the number but not the contradiction with §3.2's framing.
findings.verifier_note: The wording problem is real: §3.2 calls compactness 'a genuinely independent spatial signal' while §5.1 measures r = -0.44 between s_struct and s_compact, the two components carrying wS + wC = 0.80 of the weight. But 'the two statements cannot both hold' and 'no analysis of why |r| = 0.44 is acceptable' both overreach. First, the paper discloses the correlation twice, in §5.1 as 'one residual issue' and in §6's first limitation bullet, and proposes a replacement ('image-pair embedding distance'), so this is a labelled limitation rather than a concealed contradiction. Second, the paper does supply a de facto answer to 'why is 0.44 acceptable': r = -0.44 shares 19% of variance against 46-83% for |r| ∈ [0.68,0.91], and the empirical consequence is the measured σ gain (0.070→0.109, 0.034→0.066). Third, the -0.44 is scoped to a subset — 'on Pico-Banana local edits' — i.e. the 69.6% of triplets that are local (§4.2), not the corpus. What survives is that §3.2's 'genuinely independent' is simply false as written, and that the paper explains the -0.44 causally ('This likely reflects Stage B mask-quality artifacts') without acknowledging that it mechanically suppresses V2's variance through the same weighted-sum cancellation V2 was designed to remove.

findings.title: Table 3 is a single run with no confidence intervals, no seeds and no significance test, yet checklist item 7 answers [Yes] on the grounds that "We present the results with confidence intervals"
findings.location: Table 3 (p8); §5.4 (pp8–9); NeurIPS checklist item 7 (p22); §3.1 (p3)
findings.evidence: Checklist item 7, "Does the paper report error bars ... or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments?" Answer: [Yes]. Justification: "We present the results with confidence intervals and calibrate the thresholds." The only interval anywhere in the paper is §3.1's mask-IoU result: "improving MagicBrush dev IoU by 1.3 points over the best two-signal subset (paired bootstrap p <10−4, 95% CI[0.0085,0.0164])." Table 3 contains eight point estimates and no dispersion of any kind; §5.4 describes "one base VLM, one fine-tuning setup, and one held-out evaluation."
findings.claim: The checklist guideline asks for error bars "at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper." The experiment supporting the main learning claim (Table 3) has none, and the cited CI belongs to a different experiment (mask IoU) that supports no claim in the abstract. Running the obvious test myself on the paper's own counts: the category difference the paper calls a "match" (119/356 vs 196/494) gives z ≈ 1.86, p ≈ 0.06 — not significant, which means the paper's directional "exceeds" language on bin and "matches" language on category are both being asserted without any test that would distinguish them from noise.
findings.why_it_matters: With n = 528 and per-field differences of 5–8 points, the entire chain-vs-label comparison sits inside the range where a single seed cannot separate the systems. The checklist answer asserts a rigor the experiments do not have, which matters both for the review and for readers who rely on checklist answers to triage.
findings.verifier_note: Verified exhaustively. A grep for 'confidence', 'bootstrap', 'p <', 'error bar', '±', 'significan' across the whole paper returns exactly one substantive interval: §3.1's 'improving MagicBrush dev IoU by 1.3 points over the best two-signal subset (paired bootstrap p <10−4, 95% CI[0.0085,0.0164]).' That result appears in neither the Abstract nor §1's list of findings, so the checklist's justification ('We present the results with confidence intervals and calibrate the thresholds', item 7, p22) cites a measurement that supports no headline claim, while the experiment that does support the headline learning claim — Table 3, plus the two-epoch numbers in §5.4 — carries eight accuracy point estimates with no dispersion of any kind, from 'one base VLM, one fine-tuning setup, and one held-out evaluation.' I independently reproduced the reviewer's test: 119/356 vs 196/494 gives z = -1.861, two-sided p = 0.063. I also ran the other two: spatial z = -1.573 (p = 0.116), bin z = +2.359 (p = 0.018). So the paper's directional language rests on differences it never tested, one of which is not distinguishable from noise.

findings.title: The joint accuracy row — the only metric requiring example-level competence — favors label-only nearly 2:1 and is never mentioned in the Interpretation; both models' joint scores sit at or below the product of their marginals
findings.location: Table 3 (p8), row "joint (all 3)"; §5.4 "Results" and "Interpretation" (pp8–9)
findings.evidence: Table 3: joint (all 3) = 1.9% for chain target, 3.4% for label-only; the extraction cells for this row are "—". §5.4 Results discusses only the three per-field rows; §5.4 Interpretation states "chain-target supervision matches label-only training on category, spatial, and difficulty classification, indicating no loss in underlying prediction quality" without referencing the joint row at all. My computation of the independence products: chain 0.225 × 0.297 × 0.280 = 1.87% (observed 1.9%); label-only 0.371 × 0.422 × 0.331 = 5.18% (observed 3.4%).
findings.claim: Table 3's 'joint (all 3)' row (1.9% chain-target vs 3.4% label-only) is never mentioned in §5.4's Results or Interpretation, and because the row carries no extraction column, the paper's parseability control cannot be applied to it. That is a reporting gap the authors should close rather than a counterexample: with per-field recalls of 67.4/79.9/68.6%, chain-target's all-three-parse rate lies in [15.9%, 67.4%], so its conditional joint accuracy is anywhere in 2.8-11.9% against label-only's 3.6% — and the raw difference is 10 vs 18 of 528 examples (p ≈ 0.13). The paper should report a joint extraction rate and conditional joint accuracy.
findings.why_it_matters: The Interpretation generalizes from three individually-conditioned per-field numbers to "no loss in underlying prediction quality." The joint row is the direct test of that generalization and it points the other way. Omitting it from the discussion while reporting it in the table is a selective-reading problem, not a presentation choice.
findings.verifier_note: The verifiable parts are the numbers and the omission: Table 3 gives joint 1.9% vs 3.4% with '—' in both extraction cells, §5.4 Results discusses only the three per-field rows, and §5.4 Interpretation never mentions the joint row. The independence products also reproduce (0.225·0.297·0.280 = 1.87%; 0.371·0.422·0.331 = 5.18%). But the finding's central inference — that the joint row 'contradicts' the parseability defense — does not survive. Applying the paper's own control, chain-target's all-three-parse rate is bounded by the Fréchet range [0.159, 0.674] given per-field recalls of 0.674/0.799/0.686 (0.369 under independence), so its conditional joint accuracy lies somewhere in 2.8-11.9% against label-only's 3.4/0.936 = 3.6% — straddling it, and exceeding it under the independence assumption (5.1% vs 3.6%). The 'contradiction' is therefore unestablished, and it is a reporting gap, not a hidden result. The '44% relative deficit' is also 10 vs 18 examples out of 528 (z = 1.53, p = 0.13), so the effect size language is inflated.

findings.title: The threshold-calibration observation escalates from "suggesting" in §5.2 to "indicating" in the intro to "showing" in the conclusion, and is close to a mathematical consequence of the calibration procedure rather than an empirical finding
findings.location: Table 2 caption and §5.2 (p7); §1 (p2); Contribution (iii) (p2); §7 (p9)
findings.evidence: Table 2 caption: "suggesting that τ primarily compensates for max-pool inflation rather than signal-specific artifacts." §5.2: "This reflects elementwise max-pooling, which monotonically increases the per-pair diff mean." §1: "threshold shifts track changes in mean combined diff signal, indicating compensation for max-pool inflation rather than signal-specific artifacts." §7: "threshold offsets across signal stacks track combined-diff means, showing that calibration mainly corrects max-pool inflation rather than signal-specific quirks (§5.2)." Table 2: three rows only (n = 3 signal stacks), with Path-1 rates of 28.4%, 29.1%, 30.4%.
findings.claim: τ is chosen to hold the Path-1 global rate near a fixed target ("calibrate τ to produce a ∼30% Path-1 global rate"). If the diff-mean distribution shifts approximately by location across stacks, a quantile-matched threshold must shift by approximately the same amount — so "Δτ ≈ Δcdm.mean" is largely entailed by the calibration rule, not discovered from data. The paper never separates the max-pool explanation from the alternative that LPIPS/SSIM simply have higher individual means (no per-signal means are reported), and the calibration is not even exactly rate-matched (28.4/29.1/30.4%). Presenting this as a validated mechanism with n = 3 stacks, and hardening the verb from "suggesting" to "showing" between §5.2 and the conclusion, overstates what was established.
findings.why_it_matters: This is one of three headline construction findings in Contribution (iii) and in §7. The body's own hedge is the honest one; the conclusion's "showing" is not, and a reader who reads only the abstract/conclusion would take a near-tautology plus three data points as a demonstrated mechanism.
findings.verifier_note: Every element checks. The calibration rule is stated as a rate target: §5.2 'calibrate τ to produce a ∼30% Path-1 global rate on Pico-Banana', §3.1 'We calibrate τ to target a ∼30% global routing rate per dataset', Appendix C 'The user picks the τ that lands closest to the desired routing rate.' Under approximately quantile-matched calibration, Δτ ≈ Δlocation follows whenever the distributions differ mainly by shift, so the 'finding' is largely entailed by the procedure; the residual information content is only that the stacks are location-shifted rather than rescaled. The offsets reproduce (0.56-0.52 = 0.04 vs 0.465-0.429 = 0.036; 0.62-0.56 = 0.06 vs 0.530-0.465 = 0.065), and the rates are 28.4/29.1/30.4%, so the calibration is not exactly rate-matched. The verb escalation is verbatim: Table 2 caption and §3.1 say 'suggesting', §1 says 'indicating', §7 says 'showing that calibration mainly corrects max-pool inflation.' I can add a sharpening the reviewer missed: the max-pool explanation cannot even apply to the first comparison, because LAB+SSIM → LAB+LPIPS is a signal swap between two two-signal stacks, not a nesting, so §5.2's 'This reflects elementwise max-pooling, which monotonically increases the per-pair diff mean' explains only the LAB+LPIPS → LAB+LPIPS+SSIM step.

findings.title: The only quantitative mask-quality number in the paper is a relative +1.3 IoU delta with no absolute IoU reported, measured on 528 images from a corpus that supplies 0.2% of the release; the 257,725-triplet main corpus has no ground-truth masks at all
findings.location: §3.1 (p3); Appendix A, Pico-Banana adapter (p12); §4.1 (p5); Abstract (p1)
findings.evidence: §3.1: "improving MagicBrush dev IoU by 1.3 points over the best two-signal subset (paired bootstrap p <10−4, 95% CI[0.0085,0.0164])." Appendix A: "Sets provided_mask_path = None (Pico-Banana ships no ground-truth masks; Stage B synthesizes them)." §4.1: "The Pico-Banana derivation yields 257,725 triplets, each with a binary edit mask." Abstract: "Each example includes an edited image, its source image, a binary edit mask ... EditSleuth chains are generated deterministically from triplet-grounded upstream artifacts, with each statement tied to a specific computable source of evidence."
findings.claim: No absolute mask IoU appears anywhere in the paper, so §3.1's '+1.3 points over the best two-signal subset' cannot be interpreted, and that measurement exists only for MagicBrush dev (528 triplets); Appendix A confirms Pico-Banana 'ships no ground-truth masks,' so mask correctness is unmeasured on the corpus that is 99.8% of the release and 100% of the pilot training data. Since the mask supplies Step 2's area and localization and Step 3's concentration statement in every chain, plus one of the three V2 difficulty components (s_compact), the evidentiary backbone of the chains is validated only on the 0.2% slice — a gap §6 and §7 acknowledge in general terms but do not quantify.
findings.why_it_matters: The abstract's positioning against LLM-generated rationales rests on the artifacts being trustworthy. The paper does concede this in §6 ("Artifact-relative faithfulness"), which is why I score this minor rather than major — but the abstract and §2 ("auditable end-to-end") do not carry that qualifier, and the single quantitative mask result is too thin to support the framing.
findings.verifier_note: The absence claims verify: a grep for 'IoU' finds one substantive occurrence, §3.1's relative '1.3 points over the best two-signal subset', with no absolute IoU anywhere in the paper, and Appendix A confirms 'Sets provided_mask_path = None (Pico-Banana ships no ground-truth masks; Stage B synthesizes them),' so the 99.8% of the release that is Pico-Banana (528/257,725 = 0.2%) and 100% of the pilot training data has no reference masks. But the finding contains a factual error that a rebuttal would seize on: mask-derived quantities feed one of the three V2 difficulty components, not two. §3.2 gives D = wS·s_struct + wC·s_compact + wI·s_instr, where s_struct = 1 - SSIM(I_real, I_edited) is computed from the image pair and s_instr from the instruction; only s_compact = 1 - compactness(M) uses the mask. The chain-text part is right — Step 2's area and localization and Step 3's concentration language are mask-derived in every chain. The paper also discloses the general issue in §6 ('these artifacts are themselves outputs of computational stages. A small human-annotated audit set is a natural next step') and §7, which tempers the severity.

findings.title: The abstract's "each statement tied to a specific computable source of evidence" is contradicted by §3.4 and Appendix B: one of the six steps is a hand-authored category template with no per-triplet computation
findings.location: Abstract (p1); §3.4 (p5); Appendix B / Table 4 (pp12–13); Appendix D preamble (p14)
findings.evidence: Abstract: "EditSleuth chains are generated deterministically from triplet-grounded upstream artifacts, with each statement tied to a specific computable source of evidence." §3.4: "Category-level priors describe typical forensic signatures for the predicted edit type, using one of 12 hand-curated templates." Appendix D preamble: "Steps 1–4 and Step 6 are triplet-grounded; Step 5 is the category-level forensic prior from Appendix B." Appendix B: "All templates are phrased as category-level facts."
findings.claim: Step 5 of every six-step chain — one sixth of the supervision text — is a fixed hand-written sentence keyed only on a category label, with no computable per-triplet source. The body is explicit and careful about this two-tier structure; the abstract's universal quantifier ("each statement") drops it.
findings.why_it_matters: The abstract is where the auditability claim is made to readers who will not reach §3.4. Given that the Appendix D contradictions all originate in Step 5 (see no-faithfulness-violations-vacuous), the step the abstract implicitly covers is exactly the one that is not grounded. A one-clause fix in the abstract would resolve it, which is why this is minor rather than major.
findings.verifier_note: Verified verbatim and the obvious rebuttal fails. The Abstract says chains are 'generated deterministically from triplet-grounded upstream artifacts, with each statement tied to a specific computable source of evidence,' while §3.4 defines two statement classes and says category-level priors use 'one of 12 hand-curated templates,' Appendix B says 'All templates are phrased as category-level facts,' and the Appendix D preamble states 'Steps 1–4 and Step 6 are triplet-grounded; Step 5 is the category-level forensic prior from Appendix B.' The natural rebuttal — that Step 5 is tied to the computed Stage D category, so it is 'tied to a computable source' — does not save the sentence, because the Abstract asserts the chains are generated from 'triplet-grounded upstream artifacts,' and the paper's own vocabulary explicitly classifies Step 5 as not triplet-grounded; §2 states the restricted version correctly ('each triplet-grounded claim traces to a computed upstream value'), which is exactly the qualifier the Abstract drops. Only the phrase 'one sixth of the supervision text' needs softening to 'one of six steps,' since no word counts are given.

findings.title: The reported 30.4% global routing rate is arithmetically incompatible with the paper's own category-level scope claims and with §5.2's stated justification for the calibration target
findings.evidence: §4.2: "Stage B classifies 30.4% of Pico-Banana triplets as global and 69.6% as local. photometric and style_transfer edits are global by construction, while scene_transformation is mostly global because weather, lighting, and seasonal changes affect the full scene." §5.2: "This target matches the share of Pico-Banana labels corresponding to whole-image edits, including style transfer, photometric overlays, scene transformations, and geometric canvas operations." Table 1 shares: style_transfer 16.6%, photometric 11.7%, scene_transformation 20.4%, geometric 12.7%.
findings.claim: The four categories §5.2 names as "whole-image edits" sum to 16.6+11.7+20.4+12.7 = 61.4% of Pico-Banana, more than double the ~30% target that share is claimed to justify. Worse, §4.2 is internally contradictory: if photometric and style_transfer (28.3% combined) really are "global by construction," only 30.4 - 28.3 = 2.1 percentage points of global routing remain for every other category, so at most 2.1/20.4 = 10.3% of scene_transformation can be global — flatly contradicting "mostly global" in the same sentence, and leaving essentially zero for the 12.7% geometric "canvas operations." No per-category scope cross-tab is reported anywhere, so the reader cannot tell which statement is wrong.
findings.why_it_matters: The scope label feeds the mask, the compactness term, the Stage E spatial descriptor, and the difficulty score for all 257,725 triplets. Either τ is calibrated roughly 2x too high (systematically mislabeling genuinely global edits as local) or §4.2's category narrative is false. The paper's headline dataset statistic — 30.4% global — is not a measurement at all but a hyperparameter target (§3.1: "We calibrate τ to target a ∼30% global routing rate per dataset"), yet §4.2 presents it as a finding about the data.
findings.verifier_note: I checked every number. Table 1 (p6) gives style_transfer 16.6, photometric 11.7, scene_transformation 20.4, geometric 12.7; sum = 61.4% exactly (and Table 1's counts do sum to 257,725, so the shares are trustworthy). §4.2 (p5): 'Stage B classifies 30.4% of Pico-Banana triplets as global'; 'photometric and style_transfer edits are global by construction, while scene_transformation is mostly global'. 11.7+16.6 = 28.3, so 30.4-28.3 = 2.1pp remain and 2.1/20.4 = 10.3% — the reviewer's arithmetic is exact. The only rebuttal available is to retreat from 'global by construction' to a semantic rather than Stage-B-label claim, which forfeits §4.2's explanation of its own 30.4% and concedes a mask/scope-quality problem instead. Table 2 (p7) confirms the ~30.4% figure is the actual routing rate. I found an additional independent contradiction the reviewer missed, which makes the finding harder to rebut: §4.3 (p6) attributes geometric's 62.0% hard skew to 'canvas-level transformations increase both structural change and mask dispersion', but a whole-image mask has compactness = 1 and therefore s_compact = 0, the minimum dispersion — so §4.3 requires geometric masks NOT to be whole-image, while §5.2 counts 'geometric canvas operations' among whole-image edits. Appendix D's geometric example (p16) is indeed 'scope=local', '14% of the image'.

findings.title: "Chain-target matches or exceeds label-only on two of three fields" is contradicted by the paper's own numbers: it exceeds on exactly one
findings.location: §5.4 Results and Interpretation (p8–9), Table 3 (p8), Abstract (p1)
findings.evidence: §5.4: "Conditional on successful extraction, chain-target obtains 33.4%/37.2%/40.8% on category/spatial/bin, compared with label-only's 39.7%/42.2%/33.1%. Thus, chain-target matches or exceeds label-only on two of three fields once parseability is controlled for." §5.4 Interpretation: "chain-target supervision matches label-only training on category, spatial, and difficulty classification, indicating no loss in underlying prediction quality." Abstract: "chain-as-target supervision matches a label-only baseline on classification accuracy among parseable answers."
findings.claim: Table 3's conditional accuracies place chain-target numerically BEHIND label-only on two of three fields (category -6.3pp, spatial -5.0pp) and ahead on one (bin +7.7pp), so §5.4's 'matches or exceeds label-only on two of three fields' rests on an undeclared tolerance that counts a 5.0-point deficit as a match while implicitly not counting a 6.3-point deficit as one. §5.4's Interpretation then escalates the same six numbers to matching 'on category, spatial, and difficulty classification, indicating no loss in underlying prediction quality' — an acceptance of the null that contradicts the Results paragraph's own 'two of three' hedge and that no reported statistic supports, since Table 3 carries no CI, error bar, or test. An unpaired two-proportion test (which the paper never runs) gives z = 1.9 / 1.6 / 2.3: the evidence neither establishes parity nor excludes a real deficit. Separately, conditioning on successful extraction conditions on a post-treatment outcome whose rate differs sharply between arms (67.4-79.9% vs 93.6-100%), so the conditional comparison is not matched on item difficulty.
findings.why_it_matters: This single sentence is the paper's fourth contribution ("(iv) A pilot fine-tuning study that validates chain-as-target supervision at the classification level") and propagates verbatim into the abstract and conclusion. The one field where chain-target leads is the difficulty bin — the field where, as shown separately, label-only sits exactly at chance.
findings.verifier_note: All six conditional accuracies reproduce exactly (33.38, 37.17, 40.82, 39.64, 42.2, 33.1), and the signed gaps are -6.3, -5.0, +7.7 as claimed. But the headline 'That is one of three, not two of three' misreads the paper: §5.4 says 'matches OR exceeds', not 'exceeds'. Under a statistical reading of 'matches' the authors' claim is if anything conservative — I ran the unpaired two-proportion test the reviewer invokes and get z = 1.89 (category, p≈0.06), z = 1.57 (spatial, p≈0.12), z = 2.34 (bin): neither deficit is significant, so 'matches or exceeds on three of three' would be defensible. The reviewer's own gloss that z≈1.9 'is if anything evidence of a deficit' also overreaches on a non-significant result. What survives is the undeclared tolerance, the internal inconsistency between the Results and Interpretation paragraphs, the null-acceptance, and the complete absence of any uncertainty statement. I also found a confound the reviewer missed that strengthens the corrected version: the conditional comparison conditions on a post-treatment variable whose rate differs sharply across arms (67-80% vs 94-100%).

findings.title: Table 3 reports no chance or majority-class baseline, and a trivial constant predictor beats both fine-tuned models on category
findings.location: Table 3 (p8), §5.4 Setup and Metrics (p8), Table 1 (p6), §3.2 (p4)
findings.evidence: Table 1: MagicBrush dev other = 235 / 528 = 44.5%; background_change = 11 (2.1%) with Pico-Banana count 0. §5.4 Setup: fine-tuning is "on a stratified Pico-Banana subset (ntrain ∼20,000), balanced across 11 non-other categories and three difficulty bins." Table 3 category accuracy: chain 22.5%, label-only 37.1%. Table 3 difficulty bin: chain 28.0%, label-only 33.1%. §3.2: "We compute the empirical 33rd and 66th percentiles of D on each dataset and bin triplets accordingly."
findings.claim: A constant predictor that always answers "other" scores 44.5% on the category field — higher than label-only's 37.1% and nearly double chain-target's 22.5%. Because the models are trained only on non-other categories they can never emit "other," so the achievable ceiling on this evaluation is (528-235)/528 = 55.5%, or 53.4% once the 11 background_change rows (absent from Pico-Banana entirely) are also excluded. Neither the ceiling nor any baseline is reported. Separately, because §3.2 bins by dataset-internal tertiles, MagicBrush ground-truth difficulty bins are ~176/176/176 by construction, making chance exactly 33.3% — and label-only's conditional bin accuracy is 33.1%, i.e. indistinguishable from chance. The field on which chain-target is claimed to "exceed" label-only is the one where the comparator carries no signal.
findings.why_it_matters: Without a majority-class or chance reference, none of the twelve numbers in Table 3 can be interpreted, and two of them (category, difficulty bin) are at or below trivial baselines. The paper attributes low absolute accuracy only to "noisy MagicBrush dev labels" for category, never to the structural impossibility of emitting 46.6% of the ground-truth labels.
findings.verifier_note: Verified: 235/528 = 44.507% -> 44.5%; (528-235)/528 = 55.49%; (528-235-11)/528 = 53.41%; 528/3 = 176 exactly. §3.2 (p4) 'We compute the empirical 33rd and 66th percentiles of D on each dataset', and §5.1 (p7) confirms bins are computed 'separately for each scorer, on Pico-Banana (n=257,725) and MagicBrush dev (n=528)', so MagicBrush ground-truth bins are 176/176/176 and chance is exactly 33.3% — against which label-only's 33.1% conditional bin accuracy is indistinguishable from a constant predictor. Table 1 shows Pico-Banana other = 0 and background_change = 0, and §3.3 (p4) states Pico-Banana classifies 'with zero other', so neither label appears in the ~20K training subset. I tried to refute via the authors' own caveat at §5.4 (p8): 'Absolute accuracies are limited by noisy MagicBrush dev labels ... the relative model comparison is more reliable than the absolute accuracy values.' That caveat concerns label noise only; it does not report the ceiling, does not report any trivial baseline, and does not rescue the bin comparison, since the 'relative' comparison the authors say to trust is precisely the one whose comparator sits at chance. The only softening needed is 'can never emit' -> 'effectively cannot emit'.

findings.title: Every experiment is a single run with no seeds, error bars, or significance tests, while the NeurIPS checklist claims confidence intervals are presented
findings.location: §5.4 (p8–9), Table 2 (p7), Table 3 (p8), NeurIPS checklist item 7 (p22)
findings.evidence: Checklist item 7 ("Experiment statistical significance"): "Answer: [Yes] ... Justification: We present the results with confidence intervals and calibrate the thresholds." §5.4: "The study uses one base VLM, one fine-tuning setup, and one held-out evaluation." §5.4: "Label-only improves modestly (category 37.1→39.6%, bin 33.1→34.7%) with recall near 100%, while chain-target regresses: spatial extraction recall drops 79.9→67.0%." §4.1: "Results come from one pipeline run."
findings.claim: Table 3 — the only table with sampling variability, n = 528 — carries no error bar, CI, or significance test, and the paper reports no seed count or across-run variance anywhere ('The study uses one base VLM, one fine-tuning setup, and one held-out evaluation', §5.4). The only inferential statistic in the paper is the single §3.1 bootstrap CI for a different experiment (mask IoU), so the checklist item 7 justification ('We present the results with confidence intervals and calibrate the thresholds') is materially misleading about the pilot results it is meant to cover. The epoch-budget deltas the paper interprets (+2.5pp category, +1.6pp bin) are of the same order as the eval-set binomial SE (~2.1pp) and are supported by neither a paired test on the shared 528 items nor a seed replicate, and the 12.9-point chain-target spatial-recall 'regression' (79.9 -> 67.0) has no variance estimate at all. (Table 2's statistics are exact full-corpus computations and do not require error bars.)
findings.why_it_matters: The conclusions drawn from these deltas are strong and specific — "Six-step chain format conformance is therefore harder to learn than JSON output, and the 2B LoRA model appears to plateau below label-only recall" — and they are repeated in §6 and the Conclusion. With n = 1 run per condition, no such conclusion is licensed.
findings.verifier_note: The core is true and I verified it: grepping the whole paper, 'bootstrap'/'CI' occur only at §3.1 line 177, and neither Table 2 nor Table 3 carries any interval or test; the word 'seed' never appears. But the finding's central arithmetic is wrong: the category delta is 39.6-37.1 = +2.5pp, which is LARGER than the 2.10pp binomial SE at p=0.371, n=528, not 'smaller' as claimed (only the bin delta, +1.6 vs 2.05, is smaller). The comparison is also the wrong yardstick — two models scored on the same 528 items call for a paired (McNemar) test, whose SE is smaller than the marginal SE. Two further overreaches: (a) Table 2's cdm.mean/tau/Path-1 rate are exact deterministic computations over the full 257,725-triplet corpus, not sample estimates, so demanding error bars there is misplaced; (b) the checklist justification is not simply false — the paper does present one CI (§3.1) and does calibrate thresholds — it is materially misleading rather than a misdescription. 'One seed each' is the reviewer's inference; the paper is silent, which is itself the reportable defect.

findings.title: The headline "rank-2 collapse suppresses variance" mechanism is algebraically backwards, and only absolute-value correlations are reported so the sign that actually drives the effect is never shown
findings.location: §3.2 (p4), §5.1 (p7), Abstract (p1), Conclusion (p9)
findings.evidence: §3.2: "the magnitude trio collapses to rank-2 on both datasets (pairwise |r| ∈ [0.68,0.91]), suppressing the variance of the combined score under weighted summation." Abstract: "a naive four-component difficulty formulation suffers from a rank-2 correlation collapse among magnitude features." §5.1: "The collapse is driven by the strong negative correlation between sloc = 1−mask_area_frac and the two magnitude terms ... causing partial cancellation in the weighted sum."
findings.claim: §3.2 (p4) states the mechanism without the information that determines its direction: 'the magnitude trio collapses to rank-2 ... suppressing the variance of the combined score under weighted summation' is true only because of the sign pattern disclosed two sections later (§5.1: 'strong negative correlation between s_loc = 1 - mask_area_frac and the two magnitude terms ... causing partial cancellation'); a trio correlated positively throughout would INCREASE the variance of a positively weighted sum. Because both §3.2 and §5.1 report only absolute-value ranges (|r| in [0.68,0.91]; [0.78,0.91] vs [0.68,0.85]), the signed correlation matrix that carries the entire mechanism is never shown, and no eigenvalue, determinant, condition number, or variance-explained figure substantiates 'rank-2'. This is not verifiable from the reported range: sign assignments consistent with |r| in [0.68,0.91] range from eigenvalues (2.63, 0.32, 0.05) — near rank-2 — to (2.36, 0.32, 0.32) — full rank.
findings.why_it_matters: "Rank-2 correlation collapse" is named as a finding in the abstract, the introduction, contribution (iii), §3.2, and the Conclusion. As stated it attributes the variance suppression to the wrong property, and the one quantity that would let a reader verify the real mechanism — the signs — is deliberately removed by reporting |r|.
findings.verifier_note: The textbook identity is right, but the 'backwards' framing does not survive once the sign structure §5.1 discloses is applied. If s_loc = 1 - mask_area_frac is negatively related to s_struct and s_perc, then s_loc + a*s_struct + b*s_perc ~ 0 with a, b > 0: the near-null eigenvector of the trio has all-positive loadings, so a positively weighted sum can and does land near the null direction. Rank deficiency with a positively loaded null direction genuinely does suppress the variance of a positively weighted sum — §3.2's sentence is compressed, not inverted. I also checked whether 'rank-2' is even substantiable from the reported |r| range: with (+0.91, -0.85, -0.68) the eigenvalues are (2.63, 0.32, 0.046), i.e. plausibly rank-2; with (+0.68, -0.68, -0.68) they are (2.36, 0.32, 0.32), i.e. full rank. So the label is sign-dependent and unverifiable from '|r| in [0.68,0.91]' alone — that is the durable defect, not a reversed mechanism.

findings.title: The +55%/+94% standard-deviation headline is not a scale-invariant statistic and, by the paper's own percentile-binning rule, has no downstream consequence
findings.location: §5.1 (p7), §3.2 (p4), Figure 2 caption (p7), §4.3 (p6), Abstract and Conclusion
findings.evidence: §5.1: "V2 increases score standard deviation by +94% on MagicBrush (0.034→0.066) and +55% on Pico-Banana (0.070→0.109)." §3.2: "Binning is dataset-internal so that easy/medium/hard labels remain meaningful relative to corpus statistics rather than absolute thresholds." Figure 2 caption: "V2 widens the standard deviation by +55% (σV1 = 0.070, σV2 = 0.109) and produces tertile bins separated by ∼1σ rather than by margins below noise." §4.3: "mean of 0.450 and standard deviation of 0.109, with tertile cutoffs at 0.406 and 0.504."
findings.claim: σ is not invariant to rescaling: a formula that simply multiplied V1 by 1.557 would reproduce the +55% headline exactly while leaving every tertile assignment unchanged. Since §3.2 states that binning is percentile-based, raw σ is precisely the quantity that cannot matter downstream. V1's mean is never reported on either dataset, so a reader cannot compute a coefficient of variation or distinguish a genuine dispersion gain from a scale shift, and no scale-free evidence is offered — no CV, no Spearman correlation between the V1 and V2 orderings, no bin-reassignment rate. The Figure 2 caption's supporting claim is worse: 0.504 − 0.406 = 0.098 = 0.90σ_V2, but the 33rd-to-67th percentile gap of any roughly Gaussian variable is ≈ 0.88σ of its own distribution, so "tertile bins separated by ∼1σ" is a near-tautology that holds identically for V1. Finally, the MagicBrush σ values are given to two significant figures, so "+94%" is quantized: values consistent with 0.034→0.066 span +90% to +98%, on n = 528, with no CI.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the paper's first named finding, repeated in the abstract, introduction, §3.2, §5.1, and the Conclusion. As reported it does not establish that V2 is a better difficulty score, only that it is a differently scaled one.
findings.verifier_note: Every number checks out and I could not construct a rebuttal that saves the headline. 0.109/0.070 = 1.5571 and 0.066/0.034 = 1.9412, so a pure rescaling of V1 by 1.557 reproduces '+55%' exactly; §3.2's percentile binning is invariant to any strictly increasing transform, so raw sigma cannot affect a single downstream bin. The tautology check is the strongest part and it holds precisely: (0.504-0.406)/0.109 = 0.899, while the 33rd-to-67th percentile gap of any Gaussian is 2*z(2/3) = 0.861 sigma — so 'tertile bins separated by ~1 sigma' is a property of approximate normality, not of V2, and holds identically for V1 in its own sigma units. The quantization range also reproduces: 0.0655/0.0345 = +89.9% to 0.0665/0.0335 = +98.5%. The best available rebuttal — that both V1 and V2 are convex combinations of [0,1] components so the scale is fixed by construction — fails because V1's four weights are never stated anywhere in the paper, and Figure 2's appeal to 'margins below noise' is never accompanied by any noise estimate. I confirmed V1's mean is reported nowhere (only V2's 0.450, §4.3).

findings.title: The single bootstrap CI validates a design choice applied to 257,725 triplets using 528 held-out items, and the absolute mask IoU is never reported anywhere
findings.location: §3.1 (p3–4), Appendix A Pico-Banana adapter (p12), Table 2 (p7)
findings.evidence: §3.1: "This stack captures chromatic, structural, and perceptual edits, improving MagicBrush dev IoU by 1.3 points over the best two-signal subset (paired bootstrap p < 10⁻⁴, 95% CI [0.0085,0.0164])." Appendix A: "Sets provided_mask_path = None (Pico-Banana ships no ground-truth masks; Stage B synthesizes them)." The string "IoU" occurs exactly once in the entire paper.
findings.claim: The entire ground-truth validation of Stage B — the pipeline's central artifact — is one relative IoU delta on MagicBrush dev (n = 528, 0.2% of the release): 'improving MagicBrush dev IoU by 1.3 points over the best two-signal subset (paired bootstrap p < 10^-4, 95% CI [0.0085,0.0164])' (§3.1). The absolute IoU is never reported (the string 'IoU' occurs exactly once in the paper), so the reader cannot tell whether the masks sit near 0.20 or 0.70; the 'best two-signal subset' is never named; and B is never stated although p < 10^-4 requires B >= 10,000. Per-stack IoU is never tabulated even though MagicBrush ground-truth masks make it computable for exactly the three stacks Table 2 compares. §6 acknowledges that faithfulness is artifact-relative but reports no measurement of artifact correctness.
findings.why_it_matters: The masks determine mask area fraction, the compactness term, the spatial descriptor, the scope label, and the difficulty score — i.e. four of the six chain steps. §6 acknowledges "Artifact-relative faithfulness" as a limitation but frames it as a future audit-set issue; the more immediate problem is that mask quality has literally never been measured on the primary corpus and the one measurement that exists is unreportable in absolute terms.
findings.verifier_note: I verified that 'IoU' occurs exactly once in the paper (§3.1, line 177) and that this is the only CI/p-value anywhere, so the absolute IoU, the identity of 'the best two-signal subset', and B are all genuinely missing. But two sub-claims are answerable. First, the complaint that 'Table 2 ... omits IoU entirely' is defeated by text the reviewer overlooked: Table 2 is 'Per-stack calibrated thresholds on Pico-Banana (n=257,725)', and Appendix A (p12) states Pico-Banana 'ships no ground-truth masks', so IoU is undefined for that table by construction. Second, 'The CI itself is wide relative to the headline: ... the true gain could be 0.85 points' is not a defect — a 95% CI of [0.0085, 0.0164] excluding zero is a positive result, and its midpoint (0.0125) is consistent with the stated 1.3 points. The 99.8% figure is right (528/258,253 = 0.20%), and §6 partially concedes it ('these artifacts are themselves outputs of computational stages. A small human-annotated audit set is a natural next step'), which blunts the framing that the gap is hidden.

findings.title: The max-pool-inflation finding rests on two threshold offsets quantized to a grid coarser than the agreement claimed, and only one of the two comparisons actually adds a max-pool operand
findings.location: §5.2 (p7), Table 2 (p7), Appendix C (p13)
findings.evidence: §5.2: "+0.04 from LAB+SSIM to LAB+LPIPS versus +0.036 in cdm.mean, and +0.06 from LAB+LPIPS to LAB+LPIPS+SSIM versus +0.065. This reflects elementwise max-pooling, which monotonically increases the per-pair diff mean." Appendix C usage block: "candidate_thresholds=[0.50,0.52,0.54,0.56,0.58,0.60,0.62,0.64]." Table 2 Path-1 rates: 28.4%, 29.1%, 30.4%.
findings.claim: The arithmetic is correct (0.56−0.52 = 0.04, 0.62−0.56 = 0.06; 0.465−0.429 = 0.036, 0.530−0.465 = 0.065), but τ can only take values on a 0.02 grid, so the claimed agreements of 0.004 and 0.005 are five times finer than the search resolution — any true offset in [0.03, 0.05] would have been reported as "+0.04." The agreement is therefore not resolvable by the experiment that produced it. Separately, LAB+SSIM → LAB+LPIPS is a substitution of one signal for another, not the addition of a max-pool operand, so it cannot be evidence for max-pool inflation at all; only the second comparison (2 → 3 signals) tests the stated mechanism, leaving n = 1. Finally the three τ values do not hold the routing target fixed: achieved Path-1 rates are 28.4%, 29.1%, and 30.4%, a 2-point drift, so part of each τ offset reflects rate mismatch rather than cdm.mean shift, and the τ that would give an exactly matched 30% rate is never reported.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the paper's second named finding, appearing in the abstract, contribution (iii), §3.1, §5.2, and the Conclusion ("threshold offsets across signal stacks track combined-diff means, showing that calibration mainly corrects max-pool inflation"). Two grid-quantized points, one of which does not test the mechanism, cannot support it.
findings.verifier_note: I re-derived all four offsets from Table 2 (p7): 0.56-0.52 = 0.04 vs 0.465-0.429 = 0.036; 0.62-0.56 = 0.06 vs 0.530-0.465 = 0.065. Appendix C (p13) pins the search grid at 0.02 spacing, and all three reported tau values (0.52, 0.56, 0.62) lie on that grid, and Appendix C explicitly ties the grid to the table ('tau = 0.62 produces a 30.4% Path-1 rate; this is the calibrated threshold reported in Table 2'), so the 'usage example' rebuttal does not hold. Each tau therefore carries +/-0.01 quantization and each tau difference +/-0.02, making agreements of 0.004 and 0.005 unresolvable — 4-5x finer than the instrument. The signal-substitution point is also correct on inspection: LAB+SSIM -> LAB+LPIPS holds the operand count at two, so it cannot test 'elementwise max-pooling, which monotonically increases the per-pair diff mean'; only the 2->3 comparison does, leaving n = 1. And the Path-1 rates (28.4, 29.1, 30.4) falsify the sentence's own premise that tau 'must rise accordingly to preserve a fixed routing rate' — the rate is not fixed. I could not refute any of the three components.

findings.title: The compactness term — V2's entire justification over V1 — is identically ≈0 for the 30.4% of the corpus routed global, and the printed formula algebraically collapses to a single ratio
findings.location: §3.2 formula (p4), Appendix D style_transfer / photometric / human_centric chains (p15–16), §5.3 (p8), §5.1 (p7)
findings.evidence: §3.2: "s_compact = 1−compactness(M), compactness(M) = |M|/|bbox(M)| · |M_largest cc|/|M|." Appendix D style_transfer (source=dataset_label): "2. The mask of changed pixels covers roughly 100% of the image and spans the entire image. 3. Structural change ... (SSIM-based score = 0.80), and the edit region is well-concentrated in a single coherent region" with "difficulty score = 0.56, instruction complexity = 0.58." §5.3: "We find no faithfulness violations."
findings.claim: §3.2's compactness is algebraically one ratio, not two separable factors: (|M|/|bbox(M)|)(|M_largest cc|/|M|) = |M_lcc|/|bbox(M)|.
