Consequently a whole-image mask has compactness = 1 and s_compact = 0 exactly, so for the ~30.4% of Pico-Banana routed global, V2 degenerates to 0.55*s_struct + 0.20*s_instr — the very term that distinguishes V2 from V1 is constant. Back-solving the V2 formula on the three Appendix D examples that must be Pico-Banana (source=dataset_label) confirms it: s_compact = 0.016, -0.008, -0.024, all zero within the examples' two-decimal rounding; this is also why the residual r = -0.44 in §5.1 is reported only 'on Pico-Banana local edits'. Relatedly, §5.3's 'We find no faithfulness violations' is scoped to numerical claims and misses a prior-vs-evidence contradiction visible in its own appendix: the Pico-Banana human_centric chain reports a mask covering 'roughly 100% of the image' in Step 2 while Step 5 asserts changes 'confined to a person, with the surrounding scene preserved'.
findings.why_it_matters: The +55% dispersion gain that motivates V2 cannot be coming from roughly a third of the corpus, so the per-subset decomposition of that gain is needed and absent. And the auto-generated prose for ~78,000 global Pico-Banana triplets contains a self-contradictory spatial claim that would be trained into any model supervised on these chains.
findings.verifier_note: The mathematics and the back-solve are exactly right and I reproduced them: (|M|/|bbox|)(|M_lcc|/|M|) = |M_lcc|/|bbox|, so a whole-image mask gives compactness = 1 and s_compact = 0; with the stated weights (0.55, 0.25, 0.20) the three source=dataset_label examples yield s_compact = 0.016, -0.024, -0.008, all inside the +/-0.035 rounding envelope implied by two-decimal display. The provenance inference is airtight (§3.3: 'Pico-Banana classifies entirely through the label path'). But the faithfulness sub-claim fails. 'the edit region is well-concentrated in a single coherent region' is a correct verbalization of compactness = 1 — a whole-image mask IS one coherent region — and §5.3 scopes its claim to numerical claims matching upstream artifacts ('all numerical claims, including mask area fraction, structural-change score, and difficulty bin, match upstream artifacts by construction'), which this does. So it is not 'a plain faithfulness violation'. There is a much better example in the same appendix that the reviewer missed: the human_centric chain (p16, Pico-Banana) says Step 2 'covers roughly 100% of the image' while Step 5 asserts the prior 'changes confined to a person, WITH THE SURROUNDING SCENE PRESERVED' — a direct prior-vs-evidence contradiction inside one chain, against §5.3's 'On Pico-Banana, where categories come from curated labels, priors are always appropriate.'

findings.title: Pico-Banana covers ten, not eleven, non-other categories; the miscount propagates into §4.3's "other nine categories" and into an infeasible training-set specification
findings.evidence: §4.1: "Pico-Banana covers all 11 non-other categories, with no category above 21% and the smallest non-zero category, text_edit, at 4.1%." Table 1 row: "background_change 0 0.0 | 11 2.1 | — — —" and its caption: "background_change is reserved for foreground-preserving background swaps, which appear in MagicBrush but not Pico-Banana." §4.3: "The other nine categories are more evenly distributed, with no bin exceeding ∼40% within a category." §5.4: "balanced across 11 non-other categories and three difficulty bins."
findings.claim: Table 1 and its own caption show background_change at 0 for Pico-Banana, so coverage is 10 of 11 non-other categories, not all 11. The same error recurs in §4.3: excluding geometric and text_edit from the ten categories with defined difficulty distributions leaves eight, not nine. It recurs a third time in §5.4, where a Pico-Banana training subset cannot be "balanced across 11 non-other categories" when one of those categories has zero rows. In the same §4.3 sentence, "no bin exceeding ∼40%" is contradicted by Table 1's photometric easy = 43.8% and object_replacement easy = 41.2%.
findings.why_it_matters: Individually trivial, but the §5.4 instance has a real consequence: the pilot models cannot have been trained on background_change, and MagicBrush dev contains 11 background_change rows (2.1%) that are consequently unlearnable — which, added to the 44.5% other rows, means 46.6% of the evaluation set is scored against labels the models can never emit.
findings.verifier_note: All four instances check out against Table 1, whose counts I verified sum to 257,725 and 528 exactly. Pico-Banana background_change = 0 (0.0%), so §4.1's 'Pico-Banana covers all 11 non-other categories' is false on the authors' own table, and the table caption concedes it ('appear in MagicBrush but not Pico-Banana'); the hedge 'the smallest NON-ZERO category' in the same sentence shows the authors knew a category was empty. Ten categories have defined difficulty rows, so excluding geometric and text_edit leaves eight, not §4.3's 'other nine'. §5.4's training subset 'balanced across 11 non-other categories' is impossible when one has zero rows — and this is not cosmetic, since it feeds the unreachable-label ceiling on the 11 MagicBrush background_change eval rows. I confirmed the '~40%' overstatement: of the eight remaining categories, photometric easy = 43.8% and object_replacement easy = 41.2% exceed 40%, though the '~' hedge makes 41.2% arguable and only 43.8% is a clear breach. Nothing rebuts these; they are consistent, repeated miscounts.

findings.title: The scope distribution sums to exactly 100% across two of four defined classes, with no counts ever given for ambiguous or alignment_failed, and implies zero Path-2 promotions
findings.evidence: §4.2: "Stage B classifies 30.4% of Pico-Banana triplets as global and 69.6% as local." §3.1: "scope ∈ {local, global, ambiguous, alignment_failed}" and "assign scope by mask area: global if >90%, local if 0.5–90%, and ambiguous if <0.5%. Registration failures during L*a*b* computation are logged as alignment_failed and propagated downstream." §3.4 descriptor vocabulary: "{whole_image, four quadrants, centered, scattered, alignment_failed}." Appendix C: "for typical thresholds in our datasets the post-Otsu contribution is small (<1 percentage point)."
findings.claim: §4.2 reports a two-way split ('30.4% ... global and 69.6% ... local') that exhausts the displayed probability mass over a scope variable §3.1 defines as four-valued, {local, global, ambiguous, alignment_failed}, and no count or rate for ambiguous or alignment_failed is reported anywhere in the paper. Rounding bounds those two branches at roughly 0.1% combined, which is itself a notable unstated result given that §3.1 routes any post-Otsu mask under 0.5% area to ambiguous and §3.4 keeps alignment_failed in the chain's spatial-descriptor vocabulary; the reader cannot tell whether those branches essentially never fire or whether the reported distribution was renormalised over local+global.
findings.why_it_matters: alignment_failed is a value in the Stage E spatial-descriptor vocabulary and in the schema §3.1 says is "propagated downstream," so its prevalence is a released-dataset statistic that consumers need. If it is genuinely zero, the two-path routing rule reduces to a single mean-threshold test in practice and the paper's description of Stage B overstates the machinery actually exercised.
findings.verifier_note: The observation is real — §3.1 defines scope over four values and §4.2 reports only two, summing to 100.0 — and I confirmed by grep that no count for ambiguous or alignment_failed appears anywhere in the paper. But 'leaving 0.0% for both ... across 257,724 triplets' overreads one-decimal rounding: 30.4 and 69.6 as displayed are consistent with a residual up to roughly 0.1% (~250 triplets), so the dichotomy 'either silently renormalised or two branches never fire' is a false one. The Path-2 sub-claim is weaker still: two values both rounding to 30.4% imply a Path-2 contribution below ~0.05pp, which is not a contradiction of Appendix C's '<1 percentage point' but an instance of it, and Appendix C already frames Path-1 as 'a lower bound'. The corrupted-pair sentence in §4.1 concerns a dropped record, not a scope label, so the 'never reconciled' framing does not add force. What remains is genuine under-specification, not error.

findings.title: "Roughly 1/4–1/5 of a single component's variance" is inconsistent with the only component statistics the paper reports, under either reading of "variance"
findings.evidence: §5.1: "This compresses the combined score to roughly 1/4–1/5 of a single component's variance." §5.1: "+55% on Pico-Banana (0.070→0.109)." §4.3: "s_struct has µ = 0.446, σ = 0.244; s_compact has µ = 0.323, σ = 0.258; and s_instr has µ = 0.621, σ = 0.108."
findings.claim: §5.1's 'This compresses the combined score to roughly 1/4-1/5 of a single component's variance' cannot be reproduced from any reported number. Under the only checkable substitution — s_struct, the sole V1 component whose statistics §4.3 reports (sigma = 0.244) against sigma_V1 = 0.070 — the variance ratio is 1/12.2 (understating the claim by 2.4-3.0x) and the sigma ratio is 1/3.5 (overstating by 1.15-1.43x). Neither reading yields 1/4-1/5, and the claim cannot be checked at all for V1's two dropped components (s_perc, s_loc), whose sigmas are never reported, nor for MagicBrush, for which no component statistics are given; V1's four weights and mean are likewise never stated.
findings.why_it_matters: This sentence is the quantitative core of the mechanism narrative for the V1→V2 change. As written it is not reproducible from any number in the paper, and where it can be approximately checked it does not hold.
findings.verifier_note: The two anchor computations are right: 0.070/0.244 = 0.287 = 1/3.49 and (0.070/0.244)^2 = 0.082 = 1/12.15, so §5.1's 'roughly 1/4-1/5 of a single component's variance' matches neither reading. But the finding's own quantification is wrong: the sigma reading overstates the compression by 4/3.49 = 1.15x to 5/3.49 = 1.43x, not 'by ~1.4-2x' (the variance figure, 2.4-3.0x, is correct). More importantly, there is a rebuttal the finding half-concedes but does not close: §4.3's component statistics are V2's components, whereas the claim is about V1, whose dropped components s_perc and s_loc have no reported sigma. A V1 component with sigma ~0.28-0.35 (entirely plausible for s_loc = 1 - mask_area_frac) would put the sigma ratio at 1/4-1/5 as written. So the defect is unverifiability rather than a demonstrated error.

findings.title: The joint-accuracy row cannot be reconciled with the per-field marginals under any stated assumption, and the discrepancy runs in opposite directions for the two conditions
findings.location: Table 3 (p8), §5.4 Metrics (p8)
findings.evidence: Table 3: chain-target category 22.5%, spatial 29.7%, bin 28.0%, "joint (all 3) 1.9%"; label-only category 37.1%, spatial 42.2%, bin 33.1%, "joint (all 3) 3.4%." §5.4: "counting unextractable predictions as incorrect."
findings.claim: Table 3's joint row cannot be interpreted because the paper reports no dependence structure across fields. Chain-target's joint (1.9% = 10/528) sits essentially exactly at the product of its marginals (0.225*0.297*0.280 = 1.87%), while label-only's (3.4% = 18/528) sits 1.8 points below its product (0.371*0.422*0.331 = 5.18%) — about 2.3 binomial SE on an 18-item cell. Per-field correctness on shared items is usually positively dependent, so two different regimes in the same table warrant an explanation the paper does not give; the likely driver, that 44.5% of eval rows carry an effectively unpredictable 'other' label and therefore make the category-correct subset non-representative, is never discussed.
findings.why_it_matters: The joint row is the only metric that measures whether a model produces a usable complete forensic record, and it is the one number in Table 3 that cannot be sanity-checked against the others. At 1.9% and 3.4% (10 and 18 of 528 items) it is also the row most in need of a confidence interval.
findings.verifier_note: The arithmetic is exact: 0.225*0.297*0.280 = 1.871% vs 1.9% reported, and 0.371*0.422*0.331 = 5.182% vs 3.4% reported. I also confirmed every Table 3 cell corresponds to a whole number of items out of 528 (119, 157, 148, 356, 422, 362, 196, 223, 175, 494, 10, 18), so the table is internally coherent and the joints are not fabricated. But the inferential step overreaches twice. First, positive dependence across fields is an empirical expectation, not a constraint; here there is a concrete mechanism for sub-independence — 44.5% of eval rows are 'other', which the models effectively cannot get right, so the category-correct subset (196 items) is a systematically non-representative slice. Second, the deviation is small in absolute terms: at 18/528 the binomial SE is 0.79pp, so a 1.8-point shortfall is ~2.3 SE on a cell containing 18 items. The finding is a genuine unexplained-and-unreported dependence structure, not a demonstrated inconsistency.

findings.title: Field-extraction recall is defined in a way that cannot produce the reported label-only pattern, yet every "conditional" number in §5.4 is divided by it
findings.location: §5.4 Metrics (p8), Table 3 (p8)
findings.evidence: §5.4: "We also report field-extraction recall, i.e., the fraction of generations from which each field can be parsed ... for the label-only model, we parse all fields directly from JSON." Table 3 label-only extracted column: category 93.6%, spatial descriptor 100%, difficulty bin 100%.
findings.claim: §5.4 defines extraction recall only as 'the fraction of generations from which each field can be parsed', which leaves undefined what counts as parseable for the label-only model's category field: 93.6% (34 of 528 failures) alongside 100% for two fields drawn from the same JSON object implies the failures are key-level or vocabulary-level (e.g. an out-of-taxonomy category string), not document-level. The distinction matters because all six conditional accuracies in §5.4 divide by this quantity, and because scoring a confidently-wrong out-of-vocabulary answer as 'not extracted' rather than 'incorrect' inflates the conditional accuracy of both arms. Compounding this, §5.4 states that label-only 'predicts a JSON {category,scope,difficulty_bin} triple', yet Table 3 scores a 'spatial descriptor' field whose vocabulary (§3.4: whole_image / quadrants / centered / scattered) differs from scope (§3.1: local / global / ambiguous / alignment_failed), so it is unclear that the two arms are evaluated against the same spatial target.
findings.why_it_matters: Extraction recall is the paper's explanation for the entire raw accuracy gap ("the raw gap is driven primarily by less frequent parseable outputs rather than weaker classification") and the stated bottleneck for follow-up work. An ambiguity in its definition propagates into every conditional number and into the two-epoch comparison.
findings.verifier_note: The definitional gap is real but 'impossible under the stated definition' overreaches, because the stated definition is already per-field, not per-document: §5.4 defines extraction recall as 'the fraction of generations from which EACH FIELD can be parsed'. A generation that emits valid JSON with valid scope and difficulty_bin but an out-of-vocabulary or missing category key produces exactly the observed 93.6/100/100 pattern without contradiction. So the paper is under-specified, not self-refuting. The reviewer nonetheless understates a related and sharper problem I found in the same two sentences: §5.4 says label-only 'predicts a JSON {category,scope,difficulty_bin} triple', but the field Table 3 scores is 'spatial descriptor', which §3.4 defines over a different vocabulary, {whole_image, four quadrants, centered, scattered, alignment_failed}, than scope, which §3.1 defines over {local, global, ambiguous, alignment_failed}. That casts doubt on whether the two arms are scored on the same target for the spatial row at all.

findings.title: Appendix D never states which dataset each example comes from, and nine of twelve are necessarily MagicBrush — the flagship 257,725-triplet corpus is illustrated by three chains
findings.evidence: Appendix D: "We show one example reasoning chain per canonical category. Each example is a Stage E output verbatim." §5.3: "We inspect a stratified sample of ∼50 Pico-Banana triplets ... Appendix D shows per-category examples." §3.3: "Pico-Banana classifies entirely through the label path with zero other." Appendix D per-example difficulty scores: 0.11, 0.21, 0.28, 0.10, 0.56, 0.48, 0.19, 0.13, 0.24, 0.23, 0.51, 0.16. §4.3: "tertile cutoffs at 0.406 and 0.504."
findings.claim: Only the three source=dataset_label examples can be Pico-Banana; the nine source=rule_based/fallback examples must be MagicBrush, and Appendix D says so nowhere. To be explicit about what is NOT an error here: the apparent conflict with §4.3's cutoffs fully dissolves under the §3.2 dataset-internal-binning rule. The three Pico-Banana examples respect the stated cutoffs exactly (0.48 → medium, 0.51 → hard, 0.56 → hard), and the nine MagicBrush examples are strictly monotone in bin — easy {0.10, 0.11, 0.13} < medium {0.16, 0.19, 0.21} < hard {0.23, 0.24, 0.28} — consistent with a separate MagicBrush-internal tertile split. The real problem is the unflagged corollary: MagicBrush's entire observed difficulty range (0.10–0.28) lies below Pico-Banana's easy cutoff of 0.406, so the difficulty bin means something different in training than in evaluation.
findings.why_it_matters: The pilot trains difficulty bins on Pico-Banana and evaluates them on MagicBrush dev (Table 3, difficulty bin row). If the two datasets' bins are defined over disjoint score ranges, a model that perfectly learned the Pico-Banana mapping would call every MagicBrush example "easy" and score ~33% by construction — which is exactly label-only's 33.1%. The paper attributes low absolute accuracy solely to "noisy MagicBrush dev labels" for category and never flags this label-definition shift for difficulty.
findings.verifier_note: The provenance inference is not merely plausible, it is forced, and I found a confirmation the reviewer did not use: the three source=dataset_label examples are exactly style_transfer, photometric and human_centric — the three categories with a MagicBrush count of 0 in Table 1 — while every rule_based/fallback example belongs to a category with non-zero MagicBrush coverage. §3.3's 'Pico-Banana classifies entirely through the label path with zero other' closes the loop. The reviewer's calibration checks also hold: the three Pico examples respect the §4.3 cutoffs (0.48 medium, 0.51 hard, 0.56 hard about 0.406/0.504), and the nine MagicBrush examples are strictly monotone in bin (easy max 0.13 < medium min 0.16, medium max 0.21 < hard min 0.23). I then quantified the corollary and it strengthens: those nine scores average 0.183, and with §5.1's sigma_V2(MagicBrush) = 0.066 a Gaussian tertile split predicts cutoffs of about 0.16 and 0.22 — matching the observed monotone gaps precisely. Pico-Banana's easy cutoff (0.406) lies about 3.4 sigma above the MagicBrush mean, so the two bin scales barely overlap. §5.3's 'We inspect a stratified sample of ~50 Pico-Banana triplets ... Appendix D shows per-category examples' invites the reader to treat all twelve as Pico-Banana.

findings.title: Every one of the 257,725 examples is an edit, so the dataset cannot support the detection task the introduction motivates — and the pipeline has no mechanism to represent "no edit"
findings.location: Abstract; §1 Introduction (p1); §3.1 Stage B scope definition (p3-4); §4.2 (p5); §6 Limitations (p9)
findings.evidence: Abstract: "Forensic analysis of AI-edited images requires more than binary real-versus-fake prediction"; §1: "Detecting such edits requires more than binary real-versus-fake classification: a useful forensic system should localize the edit, identify its type, and explain the supporting visual evidence." The dataset is "257,725 image-edit triplets" with no unedited examples. §3.1: "scope ∈ {local, global, ambiguous, alignment_failed}" — there is no null/no-edit scope value. §3.1: signals are "normalized to [0,1] by its per-pair 99th percentile, then combined by elementwise maximum" and then binarized "using Otsu's method". §6 lists six limitations; none of them is the absence of negatives.
findings.claim: EditSleuth contains no unedited pairs, yet contribution (i) describes it as 'forensic-detection training data' (§1) and §6's broader impact claims it 'can support forensic detectors for image authentication in journalism, legal evidence, and content moderation' — uses that require deciding whether an image was edited at all. Stage E emits a category, mask-area figure, spatial descriptor and detectability verdict for every input; no scope value or chain form expresses 'no edit', and §6's six limitations do not list this. Whether the corpus is even extensible with negatives is untested: Stage B's per-pair 99th-percentile normalization (§3.1) rescales whatever signal exists to fill [0,1] regardless of true edit magnitude, and the one route that could flag a near-empty mask — 'ambiguous if <0.5%' — has no reported incidence anywhere in the paper (§4.2's global and local shares sum to 100.0%).
findings.why_it_matters: The paper's motivating claim is that forensics needs more than real-versus-fake. But "more than" presupposes the binary decision, and the dataset removes it: the task actually supervised is "given that this image was edited, classify how." A detector trained on this data has no calibrated notion of an authentic image and would confabulate a grounded forensic chain for an unmanipulated photo — the exact failure mode that matters for the journalism/legal-evidence applications named in the Broader Impact. This is the single largest design gap and it is not acknowledged anywhere in the six-item limitations list, so it cannot be dismissed as a known-and-scoped restriction.
findings.verifier_note: The factual core checks out: §4.1 'The Pico-Banana derivation yields 257,725 triplets', both sources are editing corpora, §3.1's scope set is 'scope ∈ {local, global, ambiguous, alignment_failed}' with no no-edit value, and none of §6's six bullets (residual mask-quality coupling / rule-coverage gap / single-source corpus / artifact-relative faithfulness / pilot scope / unverified inference-time faithfulness) mentions negatives. But two parts overreach. First, the paper's opening sentence explicitly disavows the framing being attacked — 'Forensic analysis of AI-edited images requires more than binary real-versus-fake prediction' — and §2 defines the task as 'given (I_real, I_edited, t_instr), produce a forensic explanation of the edit', a conditional-on-edit explanation task for which negatives are out of scope by declared design, not oversight. Second, 'the pipeline could not produce a negative even if one were supplied' is an untested mechanistic prediction, and §3.1 does define exactly the route the finding says is missing: 'ambiguous if <0.5%' mask area. Otsu-plus-morphological-opening on a noise-only diff is not shown anywhere to exceed 0.5%. The reviewer's real evidence is that this bucket has no reported incidence (§4.2's 30.4% global + 69.6% local = 100.0%), which is an observation, not a proof of impossibility.

findings.title: The pilot evaluation is circular and has a hard 55.5% ceiling: 44.5% of the eval set carries the label `other`, which is excluded from training by construction — and neither model beats a constant majority-class predictor
findings.location: §5.4 Setup and Results, Table 3 (p8); §3.3 (p4); §4.1 and Table 1 (p5-6)
findings.evidence: §5.4: "on a stratified Pico-Banana subset (n_train ∼20,000), balanced across 11 non-other categories". Table 1: MagicBrush dev `other` = 235 rows = 44.5%; Pico-Banana `other` = 0. §5.4: "Absolute accuracies are limited by noisy MagicBrush dev labels: the set lacks curated category annotations, so "ground truth" comes from the same rule classifier with a 44% fallback rate". Table 3 category accuracy: chain 22.5%, label-only 37.1%.
findings.claim: Table 3's category column is not interpretable as accuracy, for two reasons the paper does not disclose. (a) Training is 'balanced across 11 non-other categories' (§5.4) with zero `other` examples (Table 1), while 235/528 = 44.5% of eval targets are `other`, capping category accuracy at 293/528 = 55.5%. (b) A constant `other` prediction scores 44.5%, above label-only's 37.1%, chain-target's 22.5%, and both conditional-on-parseable figures (39.7%, 33.4%) — no arm beats a constant predictor, and no such reference point is reported. The third leg, that the eval ground truth is itself Stage D regex output with a '44% fallback rate' and 'several questionable label assignments', is the paper's own §5.4 disclosure rather than a new finding — though Appendix D showing 3 of 12 showcased regex labels wrong suggests it is worse than stated, and the abstract's 'matches a label-only baseline on classification accuracy among parseable answers' carries no caveat at all.
findings.why_it_matters: Every quantitative claim in §5.4, §1, and the abstract about chain supervision rests on Table 3. If neither arm beats a trivial baseline and 44.5% of the eval rows are unwinnable by construction, the comparison carries no information about supervision format. The authors acknowledge label noise but not the excluded-class ceiling or the majority-class baseline, both of which are recomputable directly from Table 1 and cannot be rebutted.
findings.verifier_note: Legs 1 and 3 verify exactly: Table 1 gives MagicBrush other = 235/528 = 44.51%, §5.4 trains 'balanced across 11 non-other categories' on a corpus with Pico-Banana other = 0, so the ceiling is 293/528 = 55.49%, and constant-`other` at 44.5% beats label-only's 37.1% and chain-target's 22.5% (and also both conditional figures, 39.7% and 33.4%). Leg 2 is factually wrong: §3.3 states 'Pico-Banana classifies entirely through the label path with zero other', and Appendix D's Pico-Banana chains carry 'source=dataset_label' — the training chains' categories came from the hand-curated 35-label lookup, not the regex, so it is not the *same* classifier path and the described circularity does not exist as stated. What does exist (machine-generated eval ground truth) is pre-disclosed in the very sentence the finding quotes, which already concludes 'the relative model comparison is more reliable than the absolute accuracy values.'

findings.title: Difficulty bins are dataset-internal tertiles, so the training and evaluation label functions are defined on disjoint score ranges — the bin-prediction task in Table 3 is unlearnable by construction, and the reported 33.1% is exactly chance
findings.location: §3.2 Tertile binning (p4); §4.3 (p6); §5.1 (p7); §5.4 Table 3 (p8); Appendix D chain examples (p14-17)
findings.evidence: §3.2: "We compute the empirical 33rd and 66th percentiles of D on each dataset and bin triplets accordingly. Binning is dataset-internal". §4.3: Pico-Banana "tertile cutoffs at 0.406 and 0.504" and "tertile binning produces 85,909 easy, 85,908 medium, and 85,908 hard triplets." Appendix D's nine rule_based/fallback (= MagicBrush) examples sort perfectly monotonically by score and bin: 0.10 easy, 0.11 easy, 0.13 easy, 0.16 medium, 0.19 medium, 0.21 medium, 0.23 hard, 0.24 hard, 0.28 hard — implying MagicBrush cutoffs of roughly 0.14 and 0.22. Table 3: label-only difficulty-bin accuracy 33.1%; two-epoch re-run 34.7%.
findings.claim: Every MagicBrush example in Appendix D, including all three labelled `hard`, falls below Pico-Banana's easy/medium cutoff of 0.406. A model that perfectly learned the Pico-Banana mapping from visual evidence to bin would label essentially the entire MagicBrush dev set `easy` and score at the marginal rate. Since tertile binning makes that marginal exactly 1/3 by construction, chance is 33.3% — and label-only scores 33.1%, i.e. exactly chance. The disagreement is not model failure; it is the two label functions being incompatible. The effect is amplified because s_instr (weight 0.20) is a function of instruction phrasing style, and Pico-Banana's µ=0.621 (§4.3) versus MagicBrush's Appendix D values of 0.06–0.19 means roughly 0.10 of the corpus-mean gap comes from instruction style alone.
findings.why_it_matters: One of the three fields in Table 3 is measuring nothing, and it is the one field on which chain-target "wins" (40.8% vs 33.1% conditional), which is what supports the "matches or exceeds on two of three fields" claim. §5.4 attributes low absolute accuracy solely to "noisy MagicBrush dev labels" in the category field and never connects §3.2's dataset-internal binning to the cross-dataset evaluation. The cutoffs are recoverable from the paper's own appendix, so this is demonstrable rather than speculative.
findings.verifier_note: I tried to break this and could not. §4.3 gives Pico-Banana 'tertile cutoffs at 0.406 and 0.504'; Appendix D's nine rule_based/fallback (MagicBrush) chains carry scores 0.10/0.11/0.13 easy, 0.16/0.19/0.21 medium, 0.23/0.24/0.28 hard — perfectly monotone, implying MagicBrush cutoffs near 0.14 and 0.22, all nine below 0.406. The decisive step needs no distributional assumption: a triplet scoring D = 0.23 is labelled `hard` on MagicBrush and would be `easy` on Pico-Banana, because §3.2 says 'Binning is dataset-internal'. The 'Appendix D is unrepresentative' rebuttal is foreclosed by §5.1's σ_MagicBrush(V2) = 0.066: with cutoffs at 0.406/0.504 that set could not produce three `hard` chains at 0.23–0.28. The s_instr arithmetic is exact — the nine MagicBrush instruction-complexity values (0.06–0.19) mean 0.1156 against Pico-Banana's µ = 0.621, and (0.621−0.1156)×0.20 = 0.101. Label-only's 33.1% is the constant-predictor rate for balanced tertiles. The single overreach is 'the disagreement is not model failure': chain-target's conditional 40.8% on n≈362 is ~2.9 SE above 33.3%, so partial transfer is not excluded.

findings.title: The headline pilot claim — "matches or exceeds label-only on two of three fields" — is contradicted by the paper's own conditional numbers, which show chain-target worse on two of three by 5–6 points
findings.location: §5.4 Results and Interpretation (p8-9); Abstract; §1 (p2); §7 Conclusion (p9)
findings.evidence: §5.4: "Conditional on successful extraction, chain-target obtains 33.4%/37.2%/40.8% on category/spatial/bin, compared with label-only's 39.7%/42.2%/33.1%. Thus, chain-target matches or exceeds label-only on two of three fields once parseability is controlled for". Differences: category −6.3, spatial −5.0, bin +7.7. Abstract: "chain-as-target supervision matches a label-only baseline on classification accuracy among parseable answers". §5.4 Interpretation: "chain-target supervision matches label-only training on category, spatial, and difficulty classification, indicating no loss in underlying prediction quality."
findings.claim: §5.4 hedges to 'matches or exceeds ... on two of three fields', but only one of three point estimates favours chain-target (bin, +7.7); category and spatial are −6.3 and −5.0. No test or interval accompanies any Table 3 cell, so 'matches' is asserted rather than shown — an equivalence claim requires an equivalence test, and by two-proportion computation the adverse gaps are only 1.6–1.9 SE, i.e. neither clearly losses nor demonstrated matches. The abstract ('matches a label-only baseline on classification accuracy among parseable answers') and §5.4's Interpretation ('matches label-only training on category, spatial, and difficulty classification, indicating no loss in underlying prediction quality') drop even the two-of-three hedge and are unsupported. Separately, conditioning on parseability conditions on a post-treatment, model-dependent variable — chain-target is scored on the 67–80% of rows it could parse, label-only on 94–100% — so the conditional comparison is not identified; the two-epoch re-run, where recall falls 79.9→67.0% and conditional spatial accuracy falls 37.2→32.5%, shows the selected subset is not stable across runs.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the load-bearing empirical claim of the pilot, repeated verbatim in the abstract, §1, §5.4, and §7. It is arithmetically refuted by the sentence immediately preceding it. Table 3's joint accuracies (1.9% chain, 3.4% label-only) further show neither system produces a coherent three-field forensic report even once in 25 attempts, which is incompatible with "no loss in underlying prediction quality".
findings.verifier_note: The arithmetic is right (33.4 vs 39.7 = −6.3; 37.2 vs 42.2 = −5.0; 40.8 vs 33.1 = +7.7), and Table 3's raw/extracted pairs reproduce the conditionals exactly (22.5/67.4 = 33.4, etc.). But the headline '"Two of three" is simply not what the numbers say' is the weakest available reading, because the paper wrote 'matches **or exceeds**'. I ran the tests the paper omitted: with conditional denominators 356 (category), 422 (spatial), 362 (bin) against label-only's 494/528/528, unpaired two-proportion z-scores are 1.89 (category, p≈0.06), 1.57 (spatial, p≈0.12), and −2.34 favouring chain-target on bin (p≈0.02). Neither adverse gap is significant at 0.05, so on a significance reading the authors' claim is if anything conservative and a rebuttal writes itself. What survives is the escalation and the identification problem, both of which are real.

findings.title: Stage B masks are never validated against ground truth at any scale: the entire 257,725-triplet training corpus has no reference masks, and the only quantitative number is a relative 1.3-point IoU delta with the absolute IoU never reported
findings.location: §3.1 (p3); §5 (p6, four validation axes); Appendix A Pico-Banana adapter (p12); Appendix E (p17)
findings.evidence: §3.1: "improving MagicBrush dev IoU by 1.3 points over the best two-signal subset (paired bootstrap p < 10⁻⁴, 95% CI [0.0085, 0.0164])" — the only occurrence of "IoU" in the paper. Appendix A: "Sets provided_mask_path = None (Pico-Banana ships no ground-truth masks; Stage B synthesizes them)." §5 lists the validation axes as "difficulty-score ablations ... threshold calibration ... qualitative inspection of reasoning chains ... and a pilot fine-tuning comparison" — mask accuracy is not among them. Appendix E: EditSleuth masks "follow the local texture of the diff signal and exhibit irregular outlines and occasional small false-positives in texture-heavy regions". §5.1: the residual r = −0.44 "likely reflects Stage B mask-quality artifacts, where subtle diffs produce noisier, less compact masks."
findings.claim: The absolute quality of Stage B masks is unknown. A 1.3-point relative gain is compatible with an absolute IoU of 0.15 or 0.75; the paper reports neither, nor the identity of the "best two-signal subset", nor the τ used for each stack in that comparison, nor whether each stack was recalibrated before scoring. That single number is measured on 528 MagicBrush images, while the 257,725 Pico-Banana masks — the actual training corpus, the source of mask-area and compactness figures quoted in every chain, and 25% of the difficulty score — have no reference annotation of any kind. Appendix E's qualitative comparison and §5.1's own r = −0.44 diagnosis both point toward substantive mask noise, and §6 concedes "A small human-annotated audit set is a natural next step."
findings.why_it_matters: The mask is the root artifact: it determines scope, mask-area fraction, the spatial descriptor, s_compact, the difficulty bin, and Steps 2–3 and 6 of every chain. "Faithful supervision" (§3.4) means the chains faithfully report these numbers, not that the numbers are right. Without an absolute mask-quality figure on the training corpus, the reader cannot bound how much of the dataset's grounded content is correct — which is the central value proposition over LLM-generated rationales.
findings.verifier_note: I grepped the full text: 'IoU' occurs exactly once, in §3.1's 'improving MagicBrush dev IoU by 1.3 points over the best two-signal subset (paired bootstrap p < 10⁻⁴, 95% CI [0.0085, 0.0164])'. No absolute IoU, Dice, precision or recall appears for either corpus. Appendix A confirms Pico-Banana 'ships no ground-truth masks; Stage B synthesizes them', so the 257,725 masks constituting the training corpus have no reference of any kind. Every rebuttal I could construct fails: §5's four validation axes exclude mask accuracy; Appendix E is explicitly qualitative and volunteers 'irregular outlines and occasional small false-positives'; §5.1 attributes the r = −0.44 residual to 'Stage B mask-quality artifacts'; and §6's 'A small human-annotated audit set is a natural next step' is a concession, not a defense. The under-specifications also hold: Table 2's per-stack τ values are Pico-Banana-only, so the τ used for each stack in the MagicBrush IoU comparison is never reported, and because Path-1 routing assigns whole-image masks, τ materially moves IoU.

findings.title: The difficulty score is validated only against its own dispersion and a ~50-example eyeball check; it is never compared to any detector's error rate, despite every chain asserting a claim about detectability
findings.location: §3.2 (p4); §4.3 (p6); §5.1 and Figure 2 (p7); Appendix D Step 6 of all 12 chains (p14-17)
findings.evidence: §3.2 weights are given as "(w_S, w_C, w_I) = (0.55, 0.25, 0.20)" with no justification or ablation. Validation consists of: §5.1 "V2 increases score standard deviation by +94% on MagicBrush (0.034→0.066) and +55% on Pico-Banana (0.070→0.109)"; §4.3 "We qualitatively validated the bins by inspecting a stratified sample of ∼50 Pico-Banana triplets. Clear, well-localized edits typically fell in easy or medium, while saturated whole-image masks or visually diffuse edits fell in hard." Meanwhile every chain asserts detectability: "Overall, this triplet is easier than average to detect" / "harder than average to detect". §4.3 proposes the breakdown "strong performance on easy text_edit but weak performance on hard geometric" — but §5.4 never reports pilot accuracy by difficulty bin.
findings.claim: The difficulty score is never validated against any external referent of detection difficulty — no human study, no detector error rate, and, despite §4.3 proposing exactly that breakdown, no per-difficulty-bin accuracy in §5.4. Both reported validations are internal to the formula: §5.1's σ widening speaks to dispersion and bin stability, not to whether the ordering tracks detectability, and §4.3's ~50-triplet inspection ('saturated whole-image masks ... fell in hard') restates what a 0.55 weight on 1−SSIM guarantees. The component weights (0.55, 0.25, 0.20) carry no ablation. This matters because Step 6 of every chain verbalizes the score as detectability — 'easier/harder than average to detect' — and the mapping is doubtful for whole categories: geometric skews hard at 62.0% because 'canvas-level transformations increase both structural change and mask dispersion' (§4.3), while Table 4 describes its signature as the highly salient 'cropped boundaries, scaled content, or extrapolated regions outside the original frame'.
findings.why_it_matters: The category-by-difficulty cross-tab is promoted to a headline contribution in the abstract, §1 (iii), and §7 ("geometric skewing hard (62%) and text_edit skewing easy (50%)"). If the score inverts the forensic ordering for at least two of twelve categories covering 16.8% of the corpus, curriculum sampling and per-difficulty evaluation built on it are misdirected. The authors trained two models on this data and so had the ingredients for the one decisive test — per-bin accuracy — and did not run it.
findings.verifier_note: Legs 2 and 3 survive. §4.3's 'saturated whole-image masks or visually diffuse edits fell in hard' follows mechanically from D = 0.55·(1−SSIM) + 0.25·(1−compactness) + 0.20·s_instr, so it tests nothing; the weights carry no ablation (§5.1 ablates component count, not weights); §4.3 proposes 'strong performance on easy text_edit but weak performance on hard geometric' as an evaluation breakdown that §5.4 never reports; and every Step 6 verbalizes a magnitude formula as detectability. But leg 1 is wrong on its own terms: both V1 and V2 are convex combinations on [0,1] (0.55+0.25+0.20 = 1), so σ is directly comparable across them and is not scale-arbitrary, and the paper's argument is structural rather than σ-worship — §5.1 identifies partial cancellation between s_loc = 1−mask_area_frac and the magnitude terms, and Figure 2's caption claims bins 'separated by ~1σ rather than by margins below noise', a bin-stability argument the finding never engages. The text_edit illustration is also muddled: the cited Appendix D text_edit chain (SSIM-based score 0.02) is a MagicBrush example binned `hard`, so it cannot illustrate Pico-Banana's 50.4% easy skew.

findings.title: The compactness term is mathematically degenerate for whole-image masks, so roughly 78,000 global chains tell the model that a 100%-coverage edit is "well-concentrated in a single coherent region"
findings.location: §3.2 compactness formula (p4); §4.2 (p5); Appendix D style_transfer, photometric, human_centric examples (p15-16)
findings.evidence: §3.2: "compactness(M) = |M|/|bbox(M)| · |M_largest cc|/|M|" and "The components measure edit magnitude, spatial dispersion, and instruction complexity". Appendix D, style_transfer: "2. The mask of changed pixels covers roughly 100% of the image and spans the entire image. 3. Structural change relative to the original is substantial (SSIM-based score = 0.80), and the edit region is well-concentrated in a single coherent region." Step 5 of the same chain: "applied uniformly across the image regardless of original content." The identical contradiction appears in the photometric and human_centric examples. §4.2: "Stage B classifies 30.4% of Pico-Banana triplets as global".
findings.claim: For a whole-image mask, compactness = 1 and s_compact = 0, and Stage E deterministically renders s_compact = 0 as 'the edit region is well-concentrated in a single coherent region' — contradicting Step 2 of the same chain ('covers roughly 100% of the image and spans the entire image') and, in style_transfer, Step 5 ('applied uniformly across the image regardless of original content'). All three global Appendix D examples (style_transfer, photometric, human_centric) contain this contradiction; inverting the difficulty formula recovers s_compact ≈ 0 for each, confirming it is deterministic rather than sporadic, so it applies to the ~30.4% of Pico-Banana triplets routed global (§4.2), ≈78,000 supervision targets. This is a defect in Step 3's verbalizer rather than in the numeric score (extent is carried by s_struct), but the chains are the dataset's deliverable and §3.4's faithfulness claim — 'template-driven composition only states claims licensed by upstream artifacts' — is a claim about exactly this text.
findings.why_it_matters: These chains are the training target. At this scale the model is being taught an internally inconsistent mapping from evidence to prose, which is a plausible contributor to the pilot's poor format conformance. It also means the term the paper calls "a genuinely independent spatial signal" (§3.2) is semantically inverted on a third of the corpus, undermining the V2 justification. This defect is visible in the paper's own showcase examples.
findings.verifier_note: I confirmed the arithmetic independently by inverting D = 0.55·s_struct + 0.25·s_compact + 0.20·s_instr on the three global Appendix D chains: s_compact = 0.016 (style_transfer), −0.024 (photometric), −0.008 (human_centric), i.e. exactly 0 within reporting rounding, as predicted for compactness = 1. Reconstructing all twelve chains further shows Step 3's descriptor is a deterministic threshold on s_compact ('well-concentrated' ≲0.30, 'moderately concentrated' ~0.30–0.50, 'diffuse or split' ≳0.59), so the contradiction is systematic. But 'the maximum-dispersion case receives the minimum dispersion score' misreads the design: compactness = |M|/|bbox(M)| · |M_largest cc|/|M| is a solidity-times-fragmentation measure, and extent was deliberately removed — §5.1 says V1's locality term s_loc = 1−mask_area_frac was dropped precisely because it falls as edits grow and cancels against magnitude. Extent is carried by s_struct, which is 0.80/0.64/0.72 in exactly those chains, landing them at 0.56/0.48/0.51 (hard/medium/hard). The numeric score is not degenerate; the verbalizer is.

findings.title: Step 6's explanatory clause is a canned disjunction not conditioned on the chain's own component values, contradicting the abstract's claim that every statement traces to a computable source of evidence
findings.location: Appendix D object_replacement, geometric, text_edit examples (p14-16); Abstract; §3.4 (p5); §5.3 (p8)
findings.evidence: Abstract: "each statement tied to a specific computable source of evidence." §3.4: "template-driven composition only states claims licensed by upstream artifacts". Appendix D object_replacement: "3. ... the edit region is well-concentrated in a single coherent region. ... 6. Overall, this triplet is harder than average to detect, given diffuse geometry or a high-complexity instruction (difficulty score = 0.28, instruction complexity = 0.15)." The same "diffuse geometry or a high-complexity instruction" clause appears with instruction complexity = 0.19 (geometric) and 0.18 (text_edit), against a Pico-Banana s_instr mean of µ=0.621 (§4.3).
findings.claim: Step 6 asserts a cause — diffuse geometry or high instruction complexity — that the chain's own Steps 2–3 and its own reported instruction-complexity value refute. In the object_replacement chain, Step 3 says the region is well-concentrated (not diffuse) and Step 6 reports instruction complexity 0.15 (not high), yet Step 6 offers exactly those two as the explanation. The clause is selected by difficulty bin, not by the components, so it can state an unlicensed reason.
findings.why_it_matters: This is a faithfulness violation of the exact kind the dataset is built to eliminate, present in three of twelve curated showcase examples. §5.3's audit is designed not to catch it: "We find no faithfulness violations: all numerical claims, including mask area fraction, structural-change score, and difficulty bin, match upstream artifacts by construction" — the audit checks numbers, while the defect is in the causal prose. The paper's central differentiator from LLM-generated rationales is that its claims are licensed by artifacts; here they demonstrably are not.
findings.verifier_note: I could not refute this, and the paper's own numbers make it stronger than stated. Across all twelve Appendix D chains the Step 6 clause is a pure function of the bin: identical wording for all five `hard` chains ('given diffuse geometry or a high-complexity instruction'), identical for all three `easy` chains ('given clear local geometry and a low-complexity instruction'), absent for all four `medium` chains. Inverting the difficulty formula on object_replacement gives s_compact = 0.296 — the band Step 3 renders as 'well-concentrated in a single coherent region' — while s_struct alone contributes 0.55×0.32 = 0.176 of the 0.28 total (63%), so the clause names the two smallest contributors and omits the dominant one. The finding's own comparison (MagicBrush values 0.15/0.18/0.19 against Pico-Banana's µ = 0.621) is its one weak step, since those are cross-corpus. The Pico-Banana chains make the point without that flaw: style_transfer and human_centric both carry the hard clause with s_compact ≈ 0 (their own Step 3 says 'well-concentrated') and s_instr = 0.58, below Pico-Banana's own mean of 0.621 — both disjuncts false on the paper's own numbers.

findings.title: At least three of twelve Appendix D showcase chains carry category labels that contradict the paper's own taxonomy, and the resulting Step 5 priors contradict Step 2 of the same chain
findings.location: Appendix D scene_transformation, geometric, other examples (p15-17); §3.3 taxonomy (p4); Table 4 (p13); §4.2 (p5)
findings.evidence: (1) scene_transformation: "1. The edit instruction states: 'let the cabinets be made of dark wood'. 2. The mask ... covers roughly 13% of the image and is centered ... 5. Edits of this type typically exhibit globally consistent changes in lighting, color temperature, or weather effects that affect the whole scene coherently rather than any single object." — but §4.2 says "scene_transformation is mostly global because weather, lighting, and seasonal changes affect the full scene", and a material change to cabinets is attribute_change. (2) geometric: "1. ... 'make the piece of paper hanging on the wall a mirror'. 2. The mask ... covers roughly 14% of the image and is concentrated in the upper-left region. ... 4. ... classified as geometric ... (confidence 0.85). 5. Edits of this type typically exhibit canvas-level transformations such as cropped boundaries, scaled content, or extrapolated regions outside the original frame, rather than localized object edits." (3) other: "1. ... 'have there be a basket of fruit on the counter.' ... 4. The edit is classified as other, could not be determined confidently" — a plain object addition.
findings.claim: These are diagnosable regex failures, not borderline cases. The `geometric` assignment almost certainly fires on the noun "mirror" being read as the flip operation, and it is assigned the highest confidence tier (0.85) while the chain simultaneously reports a 14% localized mask — the prior and the evidence directly contradict each other within one chain. The `other` failure is instructive because the paper claims the classifier covers "conversational frames" (§3.3), and the neighbouring background_change example handles "it should be a mountain in the background" at confidence 0.75 while "have there be a basket of fruit" falls through.
findings.why_it_matters: These are the authors' hand-picked per-category exemplars, presented as "a Stage E output verbatim". A 3-in-12 visible error rate in the showcase set is a lower bound on the error rate in the 44%-fallback MagicBrush population and gives a concrete texture to the rule-coverage limitation. It also means the confidence field is not calibrated — 0.85 on a clear misclassification — which downstream consumers would reasonably trust.
findings.verifier_note: All three quotes verify and I could not dissolve the substance. 'let the cabinets be made of dark wood' → scene_transformation at confidence 0.65 is wrong on the paper's own taxonomy: Table 4 defines scene_transformation as 'globally consistent changes in lighting, color temperature, or weather effects', §4.2 says it 'is mostly global', yet this chain is scope=local with a 13% mask — and Appendix D's own attribute_change exemplar uses the identical frame ('let the apples be changed to orange slices'). 'make the piece of paper hanging on the wall a mirror' → geometric at 0.85 is contradicted inside its own chain by Step 2 ('roughly 14% ... upper-left region') and Step 5 ('rather than localized object edits'). 'have there be a basket of fruit on the counter' → other is a plain object addition, while the adjacent chain handles the equally conversational 'it should be a mountain in the background' at 0.75. The best rebuttal — §6's 'Rule-coverage gap on MagicBrush' and §5.3's 'two MagicBrush cases where keyword rules misclassified' — blunts novelty but not substance, because these regex labels are the ground truth for every category number in Table 3. The only part I would not defend is the mechanism ('almost certainly fires on the noun mirror'), a plausible hypothesis the paper does not state.

findings.title: No external baseline is evaluated: no zero-shot VLM, no published forensic detector, no majority-class or random reference, despite a dozen directly comparable systems being cited in Related Work
findings.location: §5.4 and Table 3 (p8); §2 Related work (p2-3); References (p10-11)
findings.evidence: Table 3 has exactly two columns, "Chain target" and "Label-only" — both LoRA fine-tunes of the same Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct. §2 cites explanation-producing forensic systems including "Legion: Learning to ground and explain for synthetic image detection" [Kang et al., 2025], "Fakeshield: Explainable image forgery detection and localization via multi-modal large language models" [Xu et al., 2025], "Sida: Social media image deepfake detection, localization and explanation" [Huang et al., 2025], and "Fakexplain: AI-generated image detection via human-aligned grounded reasoning" [Ji et al., 2026].
findings.claim: Table 3 contains no reference point, so no cell in it can be read as evidence that either arm learned anything: no untuned Qwen2-VL-2B zero-shot row, no constant-predictor row, no random row. The pilot framing does not cure this, because the paper draws conclusions from the table in the abstract ('matches a label-only baseline on classification accuracy among parseable answers') and in §7. The reference points computable from the paper's own numbers are unflattering: constant `other` scores 44.5% on category (Table 1), above both arms raw and conditional, and balanced tertiles put the constant rate at 33.3% on difficulty bin, which label-only's 33.1% matches exactly. A transfer evaluation on any cited explanation-producing forensic benchmark (Legion, FakeShield, SIDA, FakeXplain) is also absent, which is the natural way to show an EditSleuth-trained model is worth training.
findings.why_it_matters: For a Datasets & Benchmarks submission, demonstrating that the resource confers measurable benefit over readily available alternatives is the core evidentiary burden. §6's "Pilot scope" limitation covers scale ("one 2B VLM with LoRA, a ∼20K stratified subset") but does not acknowledge the total absence of external reference points, so this is not a scoped-and-declared limitation.
findings.verifier_note: Verified: Table 3 has exactly two columns, both LoRA fine-tunes of Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct, and grep finds no occurrence of 'zero-shot', 'chance', 'majority' or 'random' used as a baseline anywhere. But the demand for comparisons against Legion/FakeShield/SIDA/FakeXplain is largely answered by scoping the finding overlooks: §5.4 opens 'We run a small pilot ... The study uses one base VLM, one fine-tuning setup, and one held-out evaluation; larger-scale training is left to follow-up work', §6 lists 'Pilot scope' as an explicit limitation, and those four systems consume a single image rather than a (real, edited, instruction) triplet, so they are not drop-in comparanda on this task. 'No baseline of any kind' also glosses that the paper's stated comparison — chain format versus label format at matched base model, hyperparameters and step budget — is a legitimately controlled contrast.

findings.title: The §5.3 faithfulness audit is tautological by its own wording, uses n≈50 out of 257,725, and reports failures from a dataset it says it did not sample
findings.evidence: §5.3: "We inspect a stratified sample of ∼50 Pico-Banana triplets across difficulty bins ... We find no faithfulness violations: all numerical claims, including mask area fraction, structural-change score, and difficulty bin, match upstream artifacts by construction. Forensic priors are visually plausible except in two MagicBrush cases where keyword rules misclassified the edit semantics." §4.3 separately reports "a stratified sample of ∼50 Pico-Banana triplets".
findings.claim: §5.3 provides no evidence about upstream artifact correctness. Its numerical half is vacuous by the paper's own admission — 'all numerical claims ... match upstream artifacts by construction' — so it can only detect a rendering bug, never a wrong mask or a wrong difficulty score. Its one non-vacuous half, whether the category prior matches the visible edit, is reported without a denominator: the stated sample is '∼50 Pico-Banana triplets' but the reported failures are 'two MagicBrush cases', so the MagicBrush inspection's size is unknown and its failure rate uninterpretable. Appendix D independently shows 3 of 12 showcased MagicBrush-path categories are wrong, which sits awkwardly with 'two cases'. It is also unstated whether §4.3's and §5.3's ~50-triplet samples are the same set.
findings.why_it_matters: §5.3 is one of the paper's four declared validation axes and is the only inspection of chain quality. Its stated criterion is unfalsifiable for the errors that matter, and its reported result is internally inconsistent about which corpus was examined.
findings.verifier_note: The §5.3 inconsistency is verbatim and real: the sample is 'a stratified sample of ∼50 Pico-Banana triplets' yet the reported failures are 'two MagicBrush cases', so the MagicBrush inspection has no stated denominator. The tautology point holds for the numerical half, and the paper concedes it in the same sentence ('match upstream artifacts by construction'). But 'it cannot detect a wrong mask or a wrong category, only a rendering bug' is refuted by the paragraph itself: the audit's second question is 'whether category-level forensic priors match the visible edit', and it did surface two category errors — so it is not purely a rendering check. 'Essentially no power' should also be stated precisely: 0 violations in ~50 draws still bounds the violation rate below ~5.8% at 95%, and for the numerical claims the power question is moot because they match by construction. The sample-composition slip is most plausibly a writing error the authors will fix in rebuttal rather than a substantive defect.

findings.title: The reported scope distribution sums to exactly 100% with zero mass for `ambiguous` and `alignment_failed`, and equals the Path-1 rate even though Appendix C says Path 2 contributes additional global routings
findings.location: §3.1 (p3-4); §4.2 (p5); Table 2 (p7); Appendix C (p13)
findings.evidence: §3.1 defines four scope values: "scope ∈ {local, global, ambiguous, alignment_failed}" and "assign scope by mask area: global if >90%, local if 0.5–90%, and ambiguous if <0.5%." §4.2: "Stage B classifies 30.4% of Pico-Banana triplets as global and 69.6% as local." Table 2 lists the LAB+LPIPS+SSIM "Path-1 rate (%)" as 30.4. Appendix C: "The reported Path-1 rate is therefore a lower bound on the resulting total global rate; for typical thresholds in our datasets the post-Otsu contribution is small (<1 percentage point)."
findings.claim: Two of the four scope values defined in §3.1 — ambiguous and alignment_failed — are never given a count anywhere in the paper, even though §3.1 says alignment_failed is 'propagated downstream' and §3.4 lists it as one of the six Step-2 spatial descriptors, so an unquantified number of released training chains contain a descriptor the paper never characterizes. §4.2's 30.4% global / 69.6% local sums to 100.0%, bounding both remaining scopes to roughly 0.1% combined — worth stating explicitly given that Stage B's per-pair 99th-percentile normalization is designed to fill [0,1] regardless of true edit magnitude. Separately, §4.2's total global rate (30.4%) is numerically identical to Table 2's Path-1 rate (30.4%) while Appendix C states the Path-1 rate is 'a lower bound on the resulting total global rate', so either §4.2 reports the Path-1 rate as the total or Path 2 promotes essentially nothing; the paper does not say which.
findings.why_it_matters: Scope determines the spatial descriptor in Step 2 of every chain and gates which triplets are treated as global. If `ambiguous` never fires, the pipeline has no failure signal for near-null or failed edits, and any such pair silently enters the corpus with a spurious mask and a confident chain. The bookkeeping gap also means the reader cannot reconstruct which rows were routed by which path.
findings.verifier_note: The under-specification is real: I grepped, and 'ambiguous' appears only in §3.1's definition and threshold sentence, 'alignment_failed' only in §3.1 (twice) and §3.4's descriptor list — neither is ever given a count, even though §3.1 says alignment_failed is 'propagated downstream' and §3.4 lists it among the six Step-2 descriptors. But two steps of the argument do not hold. 'Occurring exactly zero times in a quarter-million pairs' is inferred from rounded percentages: 30.4 + 69.6 = 100.0 is consistent with up to roughly 0.1% (≈250 triplets) of ambiguous plus alignment_failed being rounded away, so 'exactly zero' is not established. And Appendix C does not say Path 2 'adds up to a percentage point'; it says 'the post-Otsu contribution is small (<1 percentage point)' — an upper bound satisfied by a ~0 contribution. So §4.2's 30.4% total matching Table 2's 30.4% Path-1 rate is not a contradiction, only an unresolved ambiguity about which quantity §4.2 reports.

findings.title: The ground truth for the paper's only quantitative mask number is itself produced by an unvalidated heuristic that decides when to invert MagicBrush's masks
findings.location: Appendix A MagicBrush adapter (p12); §3.1 (p3); Appendix E (p17)
findings.evidence: Appendix A: "Decodes MagicBrush's mask encoding correctly: the mask_img field is an RGB image where the edited region is painted pure black ([0,0,0]) over the target image's color content. The naive 'convert(L)>127' threshold inverts the mask. The adapter checks for all-or-mostly-black pixels pattern and inverts as needed."
findings.claim: The MagicBrush reference masks anchoring the paper's only quantitative mask-quality claim (§3.1's '+1.3 points IoU') and Appendix E's side-by-side figures are produced by an inversion heuristic described only as 'checks for all-or-mostly-black pixels pattern and inverts as needed' (Appendix A). No threshold, no inversion rate, and no validation is reported, so the reader cannot bound how often the reference is inverted, and any inverted row makes that row's IoU meaningless. Because no absolute IoU is reported either, there is no aggregate figure against which to sanity-check the reference.
findings.why_it_matters: This is a defensible engineering choice honestly documented — the concern is only that it is unvalidated while sitting underneath the paper's sole quantitative mask-quality claim. A short reliability check on the inversion rule would settle it.
findings.verifier_note: The reporting gap is real and verified: Appendix A describes the rule only as 'checks for all-or-mostly-black pixels pattern and inverts as needed', with no threshold, no inversion rate, and no spot check, and those reference masks define both the §3.1 IoU delta (the paper's only quantitative mask claim) and Appendix E's figures. But the specific failure mode is speculation the paper's own wording partly forecloses: the same bullet specifies the edited region is painted 'pure black ([0,0,0])', and an exact-equality test on [0,0,0] — the natural implementation — is unaffected by a dark scene, which produces near-black rather than pure-black pixels. The finding also does not weigh that the authors release the construction pipeline (§7), a partial answer to a reproducibility-flavoured complaint.

findings.title: The pilot omits every training and decoding hyperparameter that determines its headline result, and two NeurIPS checklist answers point at content that does not exist in the paper
findings.location: §5.4 Setup (p8); Appendices A-E (p12-19); NeurIPS Checklist items 6, 7, 8 (p22)
findings.evidence: §5.4 reports only "LoRA [Hu et al., 2022] (r = 16, α = 32; target modules {q_proj, v_proj} in language layers)" and "identical base model, hyperparameters, and step budget". No learning rate, batch size, optimizer, warmup, seed count, decoding strategy, or max-new-tokens appears anywhere in the paper. Checklist 6 answers "[Yes] ... We provide technical details in Appendix", but Appendices A–E contain adapters, prior templates, a threshold-sweep tool, chain examples, and mask figures — no training details. Checklist 7 answers "[Yes] ... We present the results with confidence intervals", but the only CI in the paper is the mask bootstrap in §3.1; Table 3 has none. Checklist 8 answers "[Yes] ... most of the construction pipeline is done in CPU", though Stage B runs LPIPS over 257,725 pairs and §5.4 fine-tunes a 2B VLM.
findings.claim: The paper's central pilot finding is that six-step chain format conformance is the bottleneck ("chain-target extraction recall remains lower than label-only recall"). Generation length limits and decoding configuration are the most direct determinants of whether a ~80–150 word chain is emitted in full and parseable, and neither is reported — so the reader cannot distinguish a learning failure from a truncated max_new_tokens. Single-run results with no seeds and no CIs on n=528 (with conditional cells of 356–422) make the 5–7 point differences in Table 3 uninterpretable.
findings.why_it_matters: Reproducibility of the pilot is not achievable from the paper as written, and the checklist affirmations are inconsistent with the manuscript's actual content, which reviewers and camera-ready checkers can verify directly.
findings.verifier_note: Every absence claim checks out under grep: the paper contains no occurrence of 'seed', 'learning rate', 'batch', 'token', 'temperature', 'greedy', 'beam' or any decoding term, and 'optimizer' appears only inside the checklist question text. The checklist mismatches are the strongest part and I could not defend any of the three. Item 6's justification 'We provide technical details in Appendix' is false: Appendices A–E are adapters, prior templates, a threshold-sweep script, chain examples and mask figures, with no training details. Item 7's 'We present the results with confidence intervals' is false for the results carrying the paper's claims — the sole CI is §3.1's mask bootstrap [0.0085, 0.0164]; Table 3, Table 2 and Figure 2 have none. Item 8's [Yes] is unsupported by any compute figure. The one part I would soften is the causal story: the extraction recalls (step 2 = 79.9%, step 4 = 67.4%, step 6 = 68.6%) are not monotone in step position, so truncation is a live hypothesis the paper cannot rule out rather than the likely explanation.

findings.title: The Positioning paragraph's load-bearing premise is contradicted by four papers the submission itself cites
findings.location: Section 2, "Image forensics datasets" paragraph and "Positioning" paragraph (p. 2); reference list pp. 10-11
findings.evidence: Section 2 asserts of the AI-era forensics bracket: "However, most retain a single-label framing, such as real/fake or edit class, without modeling edit localization or the detector's evidential reasoning." The Positioning paragraph then drops the hedge entirely: "Forensics datasets provide masks and labels but lack instruction context and reasoning chains." The bracket being characterized is "[Wang et al., 2023, Chang et al., 2025, Kang et al., 2025, Ji et al., 2026, Ye et al., 2025, Huang et al., 2025, Xu et al., 2025, Wen et al., 2026, Han et al., 2026]". The paper's own reference list gives those titles as: "Legion: Learning to ground and explain for synthetic image detection" (Kang et al., 2025); "Sida: Social media image deepfake detection, localization and explanation with large multimodal model" (Huang et al., 2025); "Fakeshield: Explainable image forgery detection and localization via multi-modal large language models" (Xu et al., 2025); "Fakexplain: Ai-generated image detection via human-aligned grounded reasoning" (Ji et al., 2026).
findings.claim: At least four of the nine works in this bracket are explicitly localization-plus-explanation forensic datasets/models, so the characterization that they lack edit localization and evidential reasoning is false on its face, and the unhedged Positioning sentence is false. FakeShield in particular ships MMTD-Set, an image-mask-description dataset built precisely to supervise a forensic VLM to localize and explain; the paper never distinguishes EditSleuth from it, or from LEGION, SIDA, or FakeXplain, anywhere in the text.
findings.why_it_matters: The entire novelty case rests on the claim that no prior forensic dataset provides reasoning-chain supervision. That claim is refuted by the submission's own bibliography, using only the titles the authors themselves typed. Because the paper never engages these four works individually, a reader cannot tell whether EditSleuth improves on them, duplicates them, or is strictly weaker (e.g., EditSleuth's chains are template fills with no human annotation, whereas FakeShield's and FakeXplain's descriptions are model- or human-derived). This is not curable by rewording; it requires an actual comparison the paper does not contain.
findings.verifier_note: I tried to refute this and could not. Reference-list titles verified verbatim at p.10-11: "Legion: Learning to ground and explain for synthetic image detection" (line 546), "Fakexplain: Ai-generated image detection via human-aligned grounded reasoning" (line 548), "Sida: Social media image deepfake detection, localization and explanation with large multimodal model" (line 560), "Fakeshield: Explainable image forgery detection and localization via multi-modal large language models" (line 563), plus a fifth, "Spot the fake: Large multimodal model-based synthetic image detection with artifact explanation" (Wen et al. 2026, line 566). All five sit inside the nine-item bracket on p.2 that the paper summarizes as "However, most retain a single-label framing, such as real/fake or edit class, without modeling edit localization or the detector's evidential reasoning." I grepped the full text: LEGION, SIDA, FakeShield, FakeXplain and LOKI appear ONLY in the reference list, never in any body sentence, so the reviewer's claim that the paper never distinguishes itself from them is exact. External verification: FakeShield's MMTD-Set is a GPT-4o-enriched "image-mask-description" triplet set spanning PhotoShop, DeepFake and AIGC-Editing domains (i.e. it explicitly covers AI-edited images with masks plus explanations); FakeXplain ships FakeXplained, 8,772 AI-generated images with human-annotated artifact bounding boxes and descriptive captions. The best rebuttal is that "most" is a hedge and that "reasoning chains" means structured multi-step chains rather than free-form descriptions. That rebuttal fails for the first sentence -- localization plus evidential reasoning is precisely what at least four of the nine cited works do, so "most" is quantitatively wrong about the bracket the paper is characterizing. It only partially rescues the Positioning sentence: those datasets genuinely do lack the edit instruction, so "lack instruction context" survives, and I therefore trim that half of the claim.

findings.title: The "first dataset to..." claim is protected by an unfalsifiable conjunction of qualifiers and is supported by no comparison of any kind
findings.location: Section 2, Positioning paragraph (p. 2); Section 3.4 (p. 5); Section 6, Limitations (p. 9); Tables 1-4
findings.evidence: "To our knowledge, it is the first dataset to combine edited-image triplets with auditable reasoning-chain supervision for forensic VLM training." The paper contains no comparison table: Table 1 is per-category counts, Table 2 is calibrated thresholds, Table 3 is pilot fine-tuning results, Table 4 is the forensic-prior templates. Meanwhile Section 6 concedes the key qualifier: "Artifact-relative faithfulness. Chains are auditable against upstream masks, difficulty scores, and category labels, but these artifacts are themselves outputs of computational stages. A small human-annotated audit set is a natural next step."
findings.claim: The priority claim on p.2 -- "To our knowledge, it is the first dataset to combine edited-image triplets with auditable reasoning-chain supervision for forensic VLM training" -- is never checked against any named competing dataset. The paper contains no comparison table (Table 1 = per-category counts, Table 2 = calibrated thresholds, Table 3 = pilot results, Table 4 = templates) and no sentence anywhere stating what MMTD-Set, FakeXplained, LEGION or SIDA annotate, so the claim rests entirely on three conjoined qualifiers the reader cannot evaluate. Its operative qualifier is also weaker than it sounds, by the paper's own definition: auditability is artifact-relative (Sec 3.4, "Faithfulness is thus artifact-relative"; Sec 6, "Chains are auditable against upstream masks, difficulty scores, and category labels, but these artifacts are themselves outputs of computational stages"), i.e. chains are guaranteed to agree with the pipeline's own uncertified outputs, not with ground truth. To their credit the authors disclose this at the point of definition rather than burying it; the defect is that the first-ness claim is asserted without a single head-to-head comparison.
findings.why_it_matters: For a Datasets & Benchmarks submission, a priority claim of this weight normally requires a dataset-comparison table (scale, source, masks, instructions, explanation type, explanation provenance, human verification). Without it, the claim is not falsifiable by a reviewer and not usable by a reader. And once "auditable" is read as the paper defines it in Section 6, the distinguishing property reduces to "generated by a deterministic template rather than an LLM" - a real design difference, but a much smaller one than "first dataset to" implies.
findings.verifier_note: The verifiable half checks out: the priority sentence is verbatim at p.2 ("To our knowledge, it is the first dataset to combine edited-image triplets with auditable reasoning-chain supervision for forensic VLM training"), and I confirmed the paper has no dataset-comparison table -- Table 1 (p.6) is per-category counts and difficulty bins, Table 2 (p.7) is per-stack calibrated thresholds, Table 3 (p.8) is pilot fine-tuning results, Table 4 (p.13) is the forensic-prior templates. But two sub-claims fail. (1) "none of which is operationally defined" is wrong: the triplet is defined explicitly as (I_real, I_edited, t_instr) in Section 1/Section 3, and "auditable" is defined operationally in Section 2 ("each triplet-grounded claim traces to a computed upstream value and is auditable end-to-end") and in Section 3.4 ("template-driven composition only states claims licensed by upstream artifacts, making numerical and categorical claims auditable end-to-end"). (2) "'Auditable' is then downgraded in Section 6" misreads the paper: the artifact-relative caveat is stated at the point of definition on p.5, not retracted late -- Section 3.4 already says "Faithfulness is thus artifact-relative: upstream biases, such as residual structural-compactness correlation (Sec 5.1), propagate into the chains and are documented." Section 6's bullet repeats that disclosure. The authors would rebut successfully on both points, so the finding as stated overreaches; the durable core is the absence of any check against a named competitor.

findings.title: Two of the three claimed changes to the Pico-Banana taxonomy already exist in Pico-Banana; the two changes that are real go undisclosed and unjustified
findings.location: Section 3.3, "Taxonomy choice" (p. 4); cross-checked against Qian et al. 2025 (Pico-Banana-400K), cited by the paper
findings.evidence: The paper: "Our taxonomy adapts the eight-category Pico-Banana grouping [Qian et al., 2025] with three changes. First, we separate photometric edits from style_transfer, since global tone, grain, and color shifts have different forensic signatures from structural texture rewrites. Second, we add human_centric for 14 person-specific, identity-preserving operations, including pose, expression, clothing, Funko-Pop, and LEGO-style edits." Pico-Banana-400K's eight top-level categories are, verbatim from the source release: "Object-Level Semantic: Add, remove, replace, or relocate objects"; "Scene Composition & Multi-Subject"; "Human-Centric: Edits involving clothing, expression, or appearance"; "Stylistic: Domain and artistic style transfer"; "Text & Symbol"; "Pixel & Photometric: Brightness, contrast, and tonal adjustments"; "Scale & Perspective: Zoom, viewpoint, or framing changes"; "Spatial / Layout: Outpainting, composition, or canvas extension".
findings.claim: Change #2 is not a change: Human-Centric is already one of Pico-Banana's eight top-level categories, with the same membership the paper describes (clothing, expression, appearance, including stylized renditions). Change #1 is also not a change at the grouping level: "Pixel & Photometric" and "Stylistic" are already two separate top-level Pico-Banana categories. Conversely, the two genuine deltas are never stated: splitting Pico-Banana's single "Object-Level Semantic" category into four (object_addition / removal / replacement / attribute_change), and collapsing "Scale & Perspective" plus "Spatial / Layout" plus object relocation into one geometric bucket - the paper elsewhere confirms this merge, describing "geometric edits, including zoom, outpainting, and object relocation" (Section 4.3).
findings.why_it_matters: Contribution (ii) is billed as "A 12-category taxonomy of image edits adapted from the Pico-Banana grouping". If two of the three claimed adaptations are inherited rather than authored, the taxonomy contribution is smaller than stated and is mis-described. Worse, the undisclosed geometric merge violates the paper's own stated criterion: it justifies splitting photometric from style_transfer because they have "different forensic signatures", yet silently merges zoom (resampling), outpainting (generated content beyond the frame), and object relocation (inpaint-plus-paste) - three forensically dissimilar operations - into one class. A reviewer cannot assess a taxonomy whose actual delta from its source is not the delta the paper describes.
findings.verifier_note: I checked the source release directly. The apple/pico-banana-400k README gives the eight top-level categories verbatim as the reviewer quotes them, including "Human-Centric: Edits involving clothing, expression, or appearance (18%)", "Stylistic: Domain and artistic style transfer (10%)", "Pixel & Photometric: Brightness, contrast, and tonal adjustments (5%)", "Object-Level Semantic: Add, remove, replace, or relocate objects (35%)", "Scale & Perspective: Zoom, viewpoint, or framing changes (2%)" and "Spatial / Layout: Outpainting, composition, or canvas extension (2%)". So the paper's Section 3.3 sentence "Our taxonomy adapts the eight-category Pico-Banana grouping [Qian et al., 2025] with three changes... Second, we add human_centric" describes as an addition a category that is already one of the eight being adapted, and "First, we separate photometric edits from style_transfer" describes as a separation two categories the source already keeps separate at the top level. The two real deltas go unstated, and both are confirmable from the paper alone: the four object-level classes (object_addition/removal/replacement/attribute_change) split the source's single "Object-Level Semantic", and Section 4.3's own words -- "geometric edits, including zoom, outpainting, and object relocation" -- show Scale & Perspective plus Spatial/Layout plus relocation collapsed into one bucket. The only sub-claim I could dent is "with the same membership the paper describes": the source reports Human-Centric at 18% while Table 1 puts human_centric at 7.8% of the 257,725 single-turn rows, so some source human-centric labels evidently route elsewhere; I therefore drop the membership assertion, which is not needed for the finding.
